docs.title: XAL Designer — Documentation
docs.text: This manual covers the XAL Designer, the visual editor used to design, configure, and publish automata in the XAUTOMATA platform.

docs.title: What you will find here
docs.text:
The manual is organized into three sections.

Concepts introduces the automaton model — what automata are, how they work, and how they relate to the XAUTOMATA platform. Read this section first if you are new to XAL.

XAL Designer is the operational guide to the editor. It explains how to open files, create and configure states and transitions, manage variables, and publish changes to a version control system.

XAL Reference is the technical reference for the XAL language. It describes the file format, all available elements, and their attributes. This section is intended for developers and the XAUTOMATA delivery team.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
The XAL Designer works with .xal files stored in a Git repository (GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket) or on your local machine. You will need access to at least one repository containing XAL files, or a file to upload directly in the browser.

Note

Some features described in this manual are not yet available. These are marked with a Coming soon notice where applicable.

docs.title: Actions and Metrics
docs.text: Actions and metrics are the two types of functions that connect an automaton to the outside world. They are defined at the automaton level and associated with individual states.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
A metric is a function that reads data from a monitored system and returns a value.

When an automaton enters a state associated with a metric, it runs the metric once. The value returned by the metric is then compared against the metric values defined on the outgoing transitions of that state — and the matching transition fires. To read the metric again, the automaton must enter the state again, usually through a self-loop.

Many metrics read the operational state of another automaton. They do this through a query, written in a SQL-like syntax, that retrieves the current global state of the target.

A metric also defines the set of values it can return, called its enumeration. Each value in the enumeration corresponds to a possible outcome — and typically to a transition that handles that outcome.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
An action is a function that performs an operation on an external system.

When an automaton enters a state associated with an action, it executes that action. Actions can interact with external systems such as ERP platforms, warehouse management systems, ticketing tools, or custom APIs.

An action does not choose the next transition: only the metric value does. An action can write its results into the Global State through its output parameters. A state with an action and no metric leaves through a transition without a Metric Value.

docs.title: How metrics and actions work together
docs.text:
A state can have both an action and a metric. The action runs first, then the metric reads the result.

The metric runs only once per entry, so a process that must wait for an external system usually splits the work in two states: one that performs the action, and one that checks the result with a metric and a self-loop until a completion or error condition is detected.

For example, in an order processing automaton:

  • An action state sends a picking list to a warehouse management system.
  • The automaton then moves to a waiting state where a metric checks whether the WMS has confirmed the picking, and a self-loop repeats the check until it has.
  • When the metric returns confirmed, the transition fires and the process continues.

docs.title: The query mechanism
docs.text:
Metrics use a SQL-like query to read the state of another automaton. The query targets a virtual table that represents the global state of a specific automaton instance, identified by a group label.

The group label is a binding mechanism that ties the query to the correct instance of the target automaton — the one running on the same monitored object as the querying automaton.

Info

The technical details of the query syntax and the group label binding are covered in the XAL Reference — Query Syntax section.

docs.title: Input and output parameters
docs.text:
Both metrics and actions exchange data with the automaton through input and output parameters. Input parameters provide values to the function from the automaton's global state. Output parameters write results back into the global state after the function completes.

To pass data to a child automaton when it starts, for example an order ID, use the input parameters of the TransitionNew instead.

docs.title: Functions that run an automaton
docs.text: An action or a metric usually runs a Java method. It can also run another automaton: the calling automaton waits in the state until the called one finishes, then receives its output values. See Automaton Families.

docs.title: When a function fails
docs.text: If the method reports a temporary error, the platform runs it again every minute, up to ten times. After that, or after a fatal error, the automaton instance stops and waits for a manual fix.

docs.title: What is an Automaton
docs.text: An automaton is the core processing unit of the XAUTOMATA platform. It defines the operational logic applied to a monitored system — what to observe, how to react, and when to trigger actions.

docs.title: The basic idea
docs.text:
An automaton models the behavior of a real-world system as a sequence of states connected by transitions.

At any given moment, an automaton is in exactly one state. When a specific condition is met — such as a metric reaching a certain value, or a time threshold being exceeded — the automaton moves from one state to another. This movement is called a transition.

Each state can have an action to execute, a metric to read, or both. Metrics read data from the monitored system. Actions perform operations on it or on external systems.

docs.title: A concrete example
docs.text:
Consider a server being monitored for CPU usage.

An automaton for this server might have three states: Normal, Warning, and Critical. When the CPU metric reports a value above 80%, the automaton transitions from Normal to Warning. When the value exceeds 95%, it transitions to Critical and executes an action — for example, opening a support ticket.

When the CPU returns to an acceptable level, the automaton transitions back to Normal.

This logic runs continuously, reacting to real conditions as they change.

docs.title: One automaton, many objects
docs.text:
A single automaton definition can run simultaneously across many monitored objects. The same CPU monitoring logic applies to every server in the infrastructure — each server gets its own running instance of the automaton, tracking its own state independently.

This is what makes automata scalable: you define the logic once, and the platform applies it wherever it is needed.

docs.title: Automata working together
docs.text:
Complex processes are often modeled as families of automata that collaborate. A parent automaton orchestrates the overall process and starts child automata to handle specific sub-tasks. The parent either follows a child by reading its state, or waits for it to finish (see Automaton Families).

For example, an IT patching process might involve a main automaton that coordinates the overall patching sequence, and separate child automata responsible for relocating databases, recycling application pools, and sending notifications at each step.

This compositional approach allows complex operational logic to be broken into manageable, reusable pieces.

docs.title: How automata relate to the platform
docs.text:
Automata do not run in isolation. They are connected to the XAUTOMATA platform through:

  • Metrics — data collected from monitored infrastructure objects and services
  • Actions — operations performed on external systems such as ticketing platforms, APIs, or notification channels
  • Dispatchers — rules that trigger notifications and external workflows based on automaton state transitions

The XAL Designer is the tool used to create and edit automata visually, without writing XML by hand.

Note

For a detailed description of the XAL file format and all available elements, see the XAL Reference section.

docs.title: Clocks and Time
docs.text: Clocks allow an automaton to measure elapsed time and make decisions based on how long it has been in a given state or waiting for a condition to change.

docs.title: What a clock is
docs.text:
A clock is a timer variable defined at the automaton level. Every clock starts from zero when the automaton starts, and again each time it is reset. Its current value can be read at any time by a transition condition.

Clocks have no unit defined in the automaton itself — the unit is specified when the clock constraint is written: seconds, minutes or hours, seconds if you set none. The value to compare with is a number, or a Global State of the automaton such as T_max_wait, so the same automaton can use different timeouts for different instances.

docs.title: How clocks are used
docs.text:
Clocks are used in two ways in transitions.

A clock constraint is a condition that must be satisfied for the transition to fire. For example:

  • clk_retry >= 5 min — the transition fires only after 5 minutes have elapsed since the clock was last reset
  • clk_handshake < T_handshake_timeout — the transition fires only if the handshake clock has not yet exceeded the timeout held in the T_handshake_timeout Global State

A transition with several clock constraints fires only when all of them hold.

A clock reset restarts a clock when a transition fires. Resets are used to measure time from a specific event — for example, resetting a retry clock every time a connection attempt fails.

docs.title: Combining constraints and resets
docs.text:
Clocks become most useful when constraints and resets are combined across multiple transitions.

A typical pattern is:

  1. A transition resets the clock when entering a waiting state.
  2. One transition fires if the clock is still within an acceptable range — keeping the automaton in the waiting state.
  3. Another transition fires when the clock exceeds the timeout — moving the automaton to an error or exception state.

This pattern allows automata to implement retry logic, watchdog timers, and escalation workflows without any external scheduling.

docs.title: Defining clocks
docs.text:
Clocks are defined at the automaton level, not at the state or transition level. Every clock used in any transition of an automaton must be declared in the automaton's clock list.

In the XAL Designer, clocks are managed from the Clock Vars panel in the left sidebar (see Clock Variables).

docs.title: Automaton Families
docs.text: Complex processes are rarely modeled with a single automaton. Instead, they are composed of multiple automata that work together — a family.

docs.title: Parent and child automata
docs.text:
In an automaton family, one automaton acts as the orchestrator. It manages the overall process flow and delegates specific tasks to child automata that it spawns at runtime.

Each child automaton has its own states, transitions, and lifecycle. A parent can start a child in two ways:

  • with a TransitionNew: the child runs on its own, and the parent follows it by reading its state;
  • with an action or a metric of type Automaton: the child runs as a step of the parent, which waits for it to finish.

This separation keeps each automaton focused on a single responsibility, making the overall system easier to understand, maintain, and reuse.

docs.title: Spawning child automata
docs.text:
A parent automaton spawns a child using a TransitionNew transition. When this transition fires, a new instance of the specified automaton is created and begins running immediately. The parent moves to the output state of the transition and goes on with its own work.

The parent can pass data to the child at the moment of spawning, through input parameters. For example, a parent managing an order process might pass the order ID and API credentials to the child automaton responsible for creating the order in an ERP system.

A TransitionNewMulti starts one child for each item of a list, for example one per database to relocate.

Once started, the child is not linked to its parent: it does not report back, and it keeps running even if the parent finishes first. It shares the parent's group label, which lets the parent find it. See Spawning Child Automata for the fields.

docs.title: How the parent monitors a child
docs.text:
Once a child is running, the parent monitors its progress through a metric. The metric reads the child's global state — specifically, its current status — using a SQL-like query on the child's table, filtered by the group label they share.

The parent transitions based on the value returned by this metric. If the child reaches a success state, the parent advances to the next step. If the child reaches an error state, the parent can retry, escalate, or abort.

docs.title: Running an automaton as a step
docs.text:
An action or a metric can run another automaton instead of a Java method (see Type Automaton). In this case:

  1. the child starts with the values set in Action Sign (or Metric Sign);
  2. the parent stays in its state and does nothing else until the child reaches a final state;
  3. the child's output values are copied into the parent's Global States, as set in Action Return (or Metric Return). For a metric, the value marked as the symbol becomes the metric value, and chooses the parent's next transition.

Use it when the parent cannot go on without the child's result. In the Process Overview, this link is drawn as a Family Tree correlation.

docs.title: Common patterns
docs.text:
Starter / Operator is a pattern used when a process must run once per event. A persistent automaton (the Starter) continuously monitors an external system for new events. When it detects one, it spawns an Operator automaton to handle that specific event. The Starter then returns to watching for the next event, while the Operator runs the full process lifecycle independently.

This pattern is common in integration scenarios — for example, spawning one Operator per incoming order from an e-commerce platform.

Coordinator / Worker is a pattern where an orchestrator automaton manages a pool of worker automata, each responsible for a single item. The coordinator spawns the workers, usually with a TransitionNewMulti, monitors their progress, and aggregates their results. This pattern is used when the same operation must be performed on multiple items in parallel.

docs.title: Automata across repositories
docs.text:
The platform does not see repositories: it sees the XAL files it loads. Every automaton of a loaded file gets its own table, and a query can read the table of any of them, whatever file or repository it comes from (see Query Syntax).

So automata in different repositories can communicate, as long as the platform loads both files. If the file of the target automaton is not loaded, there is no table to read. The same applies to the automaton started by a TransitionNew: its file must be loaded too.

In the Process Overview of the XAL Designer, an automaton that is referenced but not defined in the current repository is drawn as a cloud (see Reading the Process Overview).

docs.title: How Automata Relate to the Platform
docs.text: Automata do not operate in isolation. They are deeply integrated with the XAUTOMATA platform and interact with its entities, monitoring data, and operational workflows.

docs.title: The interpreter
docs.text: Inside the platform, automata are run by the interpreter: the component that loads the XAL files, validates them and moves each instance from one state to the next. When this manual says what the interpreter accepts or does, it describes how automata behave once they run on the platform.

docs.title: Automata and monitored objects
docs.text:
Every automaton instance is associated with one or more monitored objects in the platform — servers, network devices, services, or any other infrastructure resource.

The automaton reads metric data produced by those objects and reacts to changes in their operational state. This is what makes the automaton a digital twin of the monitored system: it mirrors the real-world behavior of the infrastructure in a structured, queryable form.

docs.title: Automata and dispatchers
docs.text:
When an automaton transitions between states, it can trigger a dispatcher. A dispatcher is an operational rule that connects a state transition to an external action — sending a notification, opening a ticket, or calling an API.

Dispatchers can themselves be implemented as automata. In this case, a dedicated child automaton monitors the parent's state and handles all outgoing communications, keeping the main process logic clean.

docs.title: Automata and metrics in the platform
docs.text:
The metrics observed by automata are the same metrics collected by the platform's monitoring probes. When a probe detects a change in an infrastructure object, that change flows into the metric, and the automaton reacts accordingly.

This connection means that automata respond to real infrastructure events in near-real time, without requiring manual intervention.

docs.title: The XAL Designer in context
docs.text:
The XAL Designer is the tool used to create and modify automata. It connects to a Git repository containing .xal files and provides a visual canvas for editing automaton logic.

Changes made in the designer are committed back to the repository through a standard Git workflow. The platform then loads the updated files.

The overall flow is:

  1. Define or modify automaton logic in the XAL Designer.
  2. Commit and push changes to the repository.
  3. The platform loads and validates the updated files.
  4. Running instances resume from the state they were in and follow the new logic. Their clocks start again from zero.

Warning

The XAUTOMATA platform validates all XAL files when it loads them. If one file does not pass validation, no automaton starts, not even those of the valid files loaded with it. The platform's check is the one that counts, regardless of what the designer displays.

docs.title: States and Transitions
docs.text: States and transitions are the building blocks of every automaton. Understanding how they work together is essential before using the XAL Designer.

docs.title: States
docs.text:
A state represents a condition or phase in the lifecycle of the monitored process.

Every automaton has exactly one initial state — the state in which it begins when first instantiated. It may also have one or more final states — states that mark the end of the automaton's lifecycle. When a final state is reached, the automaton stops processing.

All other states are intermediate states, representing the active phases of the process.

In the XAL Designer, the color of the node border and of its left stripe shows the kind of state:

Color Meaning Green Initial state Red Final state Blue Intermediate state

A state can have an action, a metric, or both. When the automaton enters the state, it runs the action first, then the metric, once each. To read the metric again, the automaton must enter the state again, for example through a self-loop.

docs.title: Transitions
docs.text:
A transition defines the condition under which the automaton moves from one state to another.

Every transition has:

  • an input state — the state the automaton must be in
  • an output state — the state the automaton moves to
  • optionally, a metric value — the specific value that triggers the transition
  • optionally, one or more clock constraints — time-based conditions that must be satisfied

When the automaton is in the input state and all transition conditions are met, the transition fires and the automaton moves to the output state.

docs.title: Choosing the next transition
docs.text:
After running the action and the metric of a state, the automaton looks at the transitions that leave it:

  • if exactly one transition is valid, it fires;
  • if the metric value matches a transition but its clock constraints do not hold yet, the automaton waits in the state until they do;
  • if no transition expects the metric value, or two or more are valid at the same moment, the automaton stops with an error.

Design each state so that every value the metric can return leads to exactly one transition.

docs.title: Transition types
docs.text:
The XAL Designer creates three types of transitions. A fourth one, TransitionX, can only be read.

Transition is the standard type. It fires when a specific metric value is observed, when a clock constraint is met, or unconditionally if no conditions are defined.

TransitionNew starts a child automaton when it fires. The parent moves to its output state, and the child runs on its own. This is how automaton families are built.

TransitionNewMulti works like TransitionNew, but starts one child for each item of a list held in a Global State of the parent.

TransitionX is an older form that combines a transition and the start of a child. The platform still runs it, but you cannot create one in the designer.

See Transition Types for how each type looks in the designer.

docs.title: Self-loops
docs.text: A transition can have the same state as both its input and output. This is called a self-loop. Self-loops are commonly used to keep the automaton in a waiting state, polling a metric until a condition changes: each time the self-loop fires, the action and the metric of the state run again.

docs.title: Min Wait and Ignore Min Wait
docs.text:
The min wait is the time, in seconds, an automaton must spend in a state before it can leave it. It is set by whoever starts the automaton: for a child automaton, it is the Target Min Wait of the TransitionNew that started it. With no min wait, or 0, nothing is delayed.

The Ignore Min Wait option exempts one transition from it: the transition can fire as soon as its conditions hold. Enable it when a transition must react at once, for example to an error.

docs.title: XAL Designer — Overview
docs.text: The XAL Designer is a web-based visual editor for creating and modifying automata defined in XAL files.

docs.title: What you can do
docs.text:
With the XAL Designer you can:

  • connect to a Git repository (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket) or work directly in the browser
  • browse and open XAL files from the repository explorer
  • visualize the relationships between all automata in a repository through the Process Overview
  • open individual automata and edit their states, transitions, and variables on an interactive canvas
  • configure state metadata, actions, metrics, clock constraints, and parameter passing
  • commit and push changes directly to the connected repository

docs.title: The interface at a glance
docs.text:
The designer is organized into three main areas.

The left sidebar provides navigation and editing tools. Its icons give access to:

Icon Panel Tree File (Explorer) Globe Global States Clock Clock Vars Microchip New State Two arrows New Transition Store Marketplace (coming soon) Sparkle AI Assistant (Arianna) User (bottom) Account, logout and dark mode

The top bar shows the connected repository and branch, the Commit & Push button, and the buttons for full immersion and the run-time instance.

The canvas occupies the central area. It displays either the Process Overview graph or the interactive diagram of the currently open automaton.

The right panel displays the configuration form for the currently selected state or transition. It opens automatically when you click on a node or edge on the canvas.

docs.title: Tabs
docs.text:
Each automaton you open appears as a tab in the tab bar, next to the Overview tab. You can have multiple automata open at the same time and switch between them freely.

A dot indicator on a tab signals that the automaton has uncommitted changes.

See The Interface for every element in detail.

Fig.1 - The XAL Designer interface on the Process Overview

docs.title: Generating a Scenario
docs.text: The scenario is the structured natural-language description of an automaton — the bridge between your intent and the XAL file. Arianna helps you build it through a conversational flow.

docs.title: Starting a chat session
docs.text:
You can start a scenario generation from two entry points:

From a free session: click New in the sessions panel, or the New chat icon (+) in the chat header if you have no sessions yet (see Chat Sessions). The session starts with no linked file. When Arianna delivers the scenario, she proposes a file name and the session takes that name.

From an existing file: right-click a .xal or .scenario.md file in the Repository Explorer and select New chat (or Open chat if you have already written in that session). The session is linked to that file and takes its name. The file can be empty. If the XAL already has automata but no scenario, see Generate Scenario from XAL.

docs.title: Describing the process
docs.text:
Type a description of the automaton's behaviour in the chat input. There are no strict format requirements — plain language works well. Include:

  • what condition or event the automaton monitors
  • what states it can be in
  • what actions or notifications it triggers
  • any timing or threshold constraints

You can describe everything at once or build up the scenario through several exchanges. Arianna asks follow-up questions when the description is ambiguous or incomplete.

If the process is already described in a document, attach it to your message instead of retyping it.

docs.title: Attaching documents
docs.text:
To attach a document, click the paperclip icon in the input box and choose one or more files. You can also drag the files from your computer and drop them on the chat.

You can attach these types of file:

  • Text: .txt and .md.
  • Office: .docx, .pptx and .xlsx. Arianna gets their text, converted to Markdown: headings, lists and tables are kept, and images and charts become a placeholder. A message tells you which files were converted.

The old Office formats (.doc, .ppt, .xls) are not accepted: save the file as .docx, .pptx or .xlsx and attach it again.

Each attached document appears in the input box with its name and size. Click × to remove it. If you attach a file with the same name again, it replaces the first one. You can send attachments with or without a message.

Fig.1 - Two documents attached, ready to send

Click the name of a document to see the text Arianna gets from it. A .txt file is shown as it is; the other documents are shown formatted. For an Office file, this lets you check what the conversion kept.

Fig.2 - The text Arianna gets from a Word document

After you send the message, the documents stay in it: click a name to see its text again.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The text of a document can be up to 200 KB. For a .txt or .md file, this is also the limit on the file.
  • An Office file can be up to 10 MB before conversion. Its converted text must still fit in 200 KB.

Attach only what you need

Arianna reads the whole conversation again at every message, attachments included. A long document makes every following answer slower. If only a part of a document matters, attach that part.

docs.title: Generating the scenario
docs.text:
When Arianna considers the description sufficient to produce a minimal scenario, she tells you in the chat, and the Generate Scenario button appears under the input box.

Fig.3 - Arianna has enough information: Generate Scenario appears

The button is not shown in the Consult skill. You can keep writing after it appears: the button stays until you click it.

Click Generate Scenario. Arianna produces a structured scenario in Markdown format. At the same time:

  • the .scenario.md file is created in the Repository Explorer: next to the .xal file for a file session, in the data/ folder for a free session. If a file with the same name already exists, a number is added, for example pump(1).scenario.md;
  • the scenario tab opens in the editor, showing the rendered scenario;
  • the skill changes to Update.

The .xal file does not exist yet: it is created when you click Generate XAL in the scenario tab, in the same folder as the scenario.

Fig.4 - The scenario tab after generation

Another folder

The data/ folder is only a proposal. To keep the files somewhere else, drag them to another folder in the Repository Explorer, or change the folder when you commit.

docs.title: Refining the scenario
docs.text:
Read the scenario in the tab. If something is incorrect or missing, describe the change in the chat. When Arianna has understood the change, the Update Scenario button appears under the input box. Click it: Arianna updates the scenario and changes as little as possible of the parts not affected. The scenario tab then shows what changed compared with the previous version.

The scenario is the source of truth

During the generation phase, the scenario is what Arianna works from. The XAL has not been generated yet — refine the scenario until it accurately describes the intended behaviour before proceeding.

When the scenario is ready, proceed to Generating XAL.

docs.title: Generating XAL
docs.text: Once a scenario is ready in the scenario tab, you can generate the XAL file with a single click.

docs.title: Starting the generation
docs.text:
Open the scenario tab and click Generate XAL in its toolbar. The green button appears when the scenario has no XAL yet, or when its XAL was uploaded and never generated by Arianna: in that case the generation replaces it.

The button is disabled while Arianna is working and while the files are reloading. When the XAL exists and the scenario has changed, the button is Update XAL: see Updating XAL.

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
Arianna works in steps. The progress card in the chat shows the current step and lists the steps already done, with their time:

  1. Generating graph: Arianna draws the automata of the scenario as a graph, in the intermediate GraphViz .dot format.
  2. Converting to XAL: the Xautomata converter turns the graph into XAL, and the XAL is validated.
  3. Adding Functions and Global States: Arianna reads the scenario again and adds the Actions, the Metrics and the Global State variables to each automaton.
  4. The XAL file is saved in the repository explorer, next to the scenario, and linked to the chat.

Fig.1 - The progress card at step 3, with the first two steps done

Click Cancel on the card to stop the generation at any step. Nothing is changed, and the chat says Cancelled: nothing was changed.

docs.title: While the XAL is generated
docs.text:
The XAL file is locked until the generation ends, so that the changes you make meanwhile are not overwritten:

  • the automaton tabs of the file are read-only and show Regenerating this automaton...;
  • in the repository explorer you cannot rename, move, delete, restore or discard the file and its scenario;
  • you cannot commit the file and its scenario;
  • you cannot connect or disconnect a repository or a branch.

You can still edit the scenario: the XAL comes from the scenario as it was when you clicked Generate XAL.

docs.title: After the generation
docs.text:
The chat confirms where the XAL was saved. The open automaton tabs of the file show the new version, and the status badge in the toolbar shows Up to date. You cannot undo a generation with Ctrl+Z.

If the XAL contains something that will not work when it runs, Arianna adds a warning in the chat and says what to fix in the Designer:

  • Actions or Metrics that no state runs;
  • transitions that wait for a value that no Metric returns;
  • Metrics with several outputs, none of them marked as the value the transitions compare.

If some Actions or Metrics run Java methods, the Java stubs are generated too, and the chat says in which file (see Java Stubs).

docs.title: Functions and Global State variables
docs.text:
In step 3, Arianna adds to each automaton:

  • the Functions: the Actions and the Metrics described in the scenario, linked to the states that run them;
  • the Global State variables listed in the scenario, shown in the Global State Variables panel.

This step runs by itself. Some values are left for you to complete in the Designer, such as the systems that the functions call.

docs.title: Automatic retry
docs.text:
If the converter rejects the graph or the XAL is not valid, Arianna receives the errors and corrects the graph, up to three attempts in all. The card shows Fixing validation errors (attempt 2/3).... Each attempt receives the errors of all the previous ones, so the same mistake is not repeated.

Step 3 also has up to three attempts. If the Functions and the Global States make the XAL invalid, for example two functions with the same Id, Arianna adds them again, with the errors as a hint.

Validation service unavailable

If the validation service cannot be reached, the XAL is saved without validation and the chat says so. Check the XAL in the Designer when the service is available again.

docs.title: If all attempts fail
docs.text:
If the three attempts fail, the chat shows the errors of all the attempts and two buttons:

  • Download XAL: the last XAL generated, even if invalid. Often a small manual edit is enough to fix it. The button is not there when the converter rejected the last graph, because there is no XAL.
  • Download .dot: the last graph, if you want to correct it by hand.

Fig.2 - Three attempts rejected by the converter: only the graph can be downloaded

You can also ask Arianna to change the scenario and then click Generate XAL again.

Note

A failed generation does not overwrite the .xal file in the repository. The previous version is kept.

docs.title: Java Stubs
docs.text:
Some Actions and Metrics run a Java method. For each of them, the Designer writes an empty method — a stub — in a Java class, so that a developer only has to fill in the code.

There is no button: the stubs follow the XAL by themselves. They are built from the XAL, not by the AI, so they do not use your API key.

docs.title: When the stubs are generated
docs.text:
The stubs are generated at two moments:

  • after Generate XAL and Update XAL: the chat says in which file;
  • when you open the commit dialog: the stubs of every XAL changed since the last commit are brought up to date. A function you added by hand in the Designer gets its method, and the .java file appears among the changes.

Fig.1 - The chat says where the stubs are

Only an XAL with an Arianna chat gets stubs. If you work on an XAL without Arianna, no .java file is created: you write the methods yourself.

docs.title: The Java file
docs.text:
There is one Java class for each XAL. Its name comes from the Class of the Actions and Metrics. Arianna gives the same class to all the automata of a scenario: xal. followed by the scenario name, for example xal.PumpStation. When the scenario has no name, the class is xal.Utils.

The file is saved in the src/ folder, for example src/PumpStation.java. If the file is already in the repository, the Designer adds the new methods to it.

To keep the file in another folder, change its folder in the commit dialog, or drag it in the file tree. The Actions and Metrics of the XAL follow the new path. The .java file does not move when you move the XAL.

The .java file is committed together with its XAL and its scenario: in the commit dialog, selecting one of the three selects the other two (see Commit and Push). Before the commit, its menu in the file tree offers Download and Remove file.

docs.title: What a stub contains
docs.text:
Each stub has:

  • a comment with the description of the state that runs the method, taken from the scenario;
  • the parameters, in this order: the result of the Query, if the function has one; the data source, if it has one; then the inputs, with the type of their Global State variable;
  • the return type: nothing for an Action without outputs, the type of the output when there is one, a map when there are several. A Metric returns a String: the value that chooses the outgoing transition;
  • in the body, a TODO, the values a Metric must return, and the inputs. Until you implement it, the method throws an exception.
XAL type Java type string String int Integer long Long bool Boolean object Object list[string] ArrayList<String> map[string,object] HashMap<String, Object>

Keep the parameter types

The platform finds the method by the exact types of its parameters. If you change Integer to int, or ArrayList to List, the code compiles, but the method is not found when the automaton runs.

docs.title: The stub in the Designer
docs.text:
Select a state and open its Action or Metric section. The Action Data or Metric Data box shows the Java file, the Class, the method, its parameters and, at the bottom, the code of the method. The code is read-only.

Fig.2 - The stub of a Metric in the Designer

docs.title: Implementing and updating the methods
docs.text:
You write the code of the methods in the .java file, outside the Designer.

When the stubs are generated again, the methods already in the class are kept as they are, implemented or not: only the missing methods are added. Keep in mind:

  • a method is recognized by its name only. If the inputs of a function change in the XAL, update the signature of its method by hand;
  • if there is no local copy of the file, the generation starts from the version in the repository, and the chat says so;
  • the methods that no Action or Metric calls any more are listed in the chat, but they stay in the file: remove them by hand if you no longer need them. The chat also tells you which of them another XAL with the same class still calls.

If no Action or Metric of the XAL has a Class, no file is written: the chat asks you to set the Class in the Action or Metric section of the node. The stubs are then generated at the next commit.

The Actions and Metrics themselves are added by Arianna while generating the XAL (see Generating XAL).

docs.title: AI Assistant — Overview
docs.text: Arianna is the AI assistant built into the XAL Designer. It helps you go from a natural-language description of a process to a valid, structured XAL file — and keeps the two artefacts in sync as either one evolves.

docs.title: The file model
docs.text: Understanding how Arianna organises its work is essential before using it. Three artefacts are always involved, and they are linked by design.

docs.title: Chat session, scenario, and XAL file
docs.text:
Every chat session is tied to exactly one XAL file. The session remembers the conversation history, the generated scenario, and the last XAL it produced. This link is permanent for the lifetime of the session: the chat always works on that file, regardless of which tab is active in the editor.

The scenario is the structured natural-language description of the automaton — the intermediate artefact between your intent and the XAL. It lives in a dedicated .scenario.md file that Arianna creates automatically.

The three artefacts form a triad:

patch_oracle.xal            ← the automaton file
patch_oracle.scenario.md    ← the scenario (satellite, same base name)
                            ← the chat session (linked to patch_oracle.xal)

One session per file

Two chat sessions cannot be linked to the same XAL file at the same time. If you open a chat for a file that already has one, the existing session is reactivated.

docs.title: The satellite file
docs.text:
The scenario file is a satellite of the XAL file: it always lives in the same directory and shares the same base name, with a .scenario.md extension instead of .xal. This co-location is structural — the link between the two is never stored explicitly; it is derived from the path.

The scenario file can exist before the XAL file (Arianna creates it as soon as the scenario is ready), but it can never exist in a different directory. When you rename or move an XAL file that is not committed yet, the scenario file moves with it and the chat session follows.

docs.title: One scenario tab at a time
docs.text:
The editor allows only one scenario tab open at a time. This is intentional: the scenario tab and the active chat session are always in sync, and having multiple scenario tabs open simultaneously would break that contract. If you switch to a different chat session, the current scenario tab is closed and the new session's scenario (if any) is opened in its place.

While you are editing the scenario, you can't switch to another one: the Designer shows the Unsaved scenario warning. Save or cancel the edit first.

docs.title: Opening a chat session
docs.text:
To link a chat session to an XAL file, right-click the file in the Repository Explorer.

The context menu entry changes depending on whether a session already exists for that file:

Entry Condition Effect Open chat The file's chat already has messages Opens the AI Assistant panel on that chat; opens the scenario tab if a scenario is present New chat The file has no chat yet, or its chat is still empty Creates a chat linked to this file, named after the file. An empty chat is reopened, not duplicated

The same entry is available on .scenario.md files: the scenario and the XAL share the same chat.

Files that are not committed yet also have Download and Remove file in the menu, and an XAL file has Rename too.

Fig.1 - The "Open chat" entry in the Repository Explorer context menu

docs.title: Arianna's introduction
docs.text:
A new, empty chat starts with a short introduction: what Arianna does, and what you need to tell her. She knows XAL and the Xautomata runtime, but not your systems, endpoints, and domain rules. The introduction disappears with your first message.

The User Guide chat shows a shorter introduction.

Fig.2 - A new chat: Arianna introduces herself

docs.title: Full screen
docs.text:
Long answers, such as a consistency report, are easier to read in full screen. Click Full screen in the chat header: the chat covers the whole window, with the same header, messages, and input box. To go back, click Exit full screen at the top right, or press Esc.

Nothing is lost when you switch: your unsent message, the skill, and an answer in progress stay as they are.

Fig.3 - The chat in full screen. The button at the top right brings it back to the side panel

docs.title: The scenario tab
docs.text: When Arianna generates a scenario, the Designer opens a scenario tab in the editor. It shows the scenario in rendered Markdown, with a toolbar above it.

docs.title: The toolbar
docs.text:
The toolbar shows only the actions that apply to the current state of scenario and XAL.

On the left:

  • the status badge: an icon that tells you whether scenario and XAL are aligned. Move the mouse over it to read the state;
  • Generate XAL or Update XAL, when the XAL is missing or behind the scenario: see Generating XAL and Updating XAL;
  • Sync Scenario, when the XAL was edited by hand: see Syncing the Scenario;
  • Verify XAL Consistency, when there is an XAL to check: see Verifying Consistency.

The table in Updating XAL lists every state with its badge and buttons.

On the right, three round buttons:

Button Effect Show changes since the last commit Shows the changes of the scenario, compared with an earlier version. It appears once there is more than one version. See Scenario History Edit scenario Opens the scenario as text. Click Save to keep the changes or Cancel to drop them. While you edit, the toolbar shows only these two buttons Focus Concentrates the workspace on this file (see below)

Fig.4 - The scenario tab. Here the scenario changed after the last generation: blue arrow and Update XAL. The mouse is on Focus

docs.title: The Focus button
docs.text:
Clicking Focus:

  1. Closes the automaton tabs of other XAL files
  2. Opens all automata defined in the linked XAL file
  3. Shows the scenario tab and opens the AI Assistant panel on the file's chat, creating the chat if there is none

Use Focus when you want to concentrate the workspace on a single file — for example, after switching between several automata and wanting a clean view of the one you are currently working on.

docs.title: What Arianna can do
docs.text:
Once a chat session is open, Arianna can help you with the following tasks. Each is covered in a dedicated page.

Task When to use Generating a Scenario You have a natural-language description and want to produce a structured scenario Generating XAL A scenario is ready and you want to generate the XAL file Updating XAL The scenario has changed and you want to propagate the changes to the existing XAL Java Stubs The XAL runs Java methods and you want to know where their code goes Syncing the Scenario You have edited the XAL manually and want to update the scenario to match Verifying Consistency You want to check that scenario and XAL are semantically aligned Generate Scenario from XAL You have an existing XAL file with no scenario and want to reconstruct one Scenario History You want to see how the scenario changed since the last commit, or bring back an earlier version Chat Sessions Managing multiple sessions, skills, and guided flows

docs.title: Generate Scenario from XAL
docs.text: If you have an existing XAL file with no associated scenario, Arianna can reconstruct one by reading the automaton structure.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
This flow is useful when:

  • you are working with a legacy XAL file that was created manually or by another tool
  • you received an XAL file and want a human-readable description of what it does
  • you want to ask Arianna questions about an existing automaton

docs.title: Starting the flow
docs.text:
Right-click the XAL file in the Repository Explorer and select New chat (or Open chat). If the file has automata but no scenario yet, the chat shows This XAL file has no associated scenario yet. and the Generate scenario from XAL button in place of the input box.

Fig.1 - A chat on an XAL file with no scenario

Click Generate scenario from XAL. Arianna reads the whole XAL and writes a structured scenario. The .scenario.md file is created next to the .xal file and the scenario tab opens.

Only questions, no scenario

If you only want to ask about the XAL, select the Consult skill in the chat header. The input box comes back and Arianna answers about the XAL's states and transitions without creating a scenario. See Skills.

docs.title: The guided verification flow
docs.text:
Reconstructing a scenario from an XAL is a reverse operation: Arianna infers the intent from the structure, and this can introduce inaccuracies, especially in complex automata. After the scenario is generated, Arianna guides you through a check:

  1. Check suggestion: a message in the chat says that the scenario was inferred from the XAL and may contain inaccuracies, with a Verify Scenario Consistency button. Until you run the check, the Verify XAL Consistency button in the scenario tab shows a dot.
  2. Consistency check: click Verify Scenario Consistency in the message, or Verify XAL Consistency in the scenario tab. The report appears in the chat (see Verifying Consistency). After the first check, the button in the message is disabled.
  3. Working direction: after the report, Arianna adds a message: The XAL is the source of truth. Any inconsistencies should be resolved by editing the scenario — not the XAL. Ask me for help refining it.
  4. Update scenario from report: click this button, under the message, to have Arianna fix the scenario where the report found differences. Only the scenario changes; the XAL stays as it is.

docs.title: Refining the scenario
docs.text:
After the check, refine the scenario by describing corrections in the chat, then click Update Scenario. The goal of this flow is a scenario that describes what the XAL does, not a different XAL.

When the scenario is accurate, switch to the Consult skill to ask questions about the automaton, or commit both files to the repository.

docs.title: Scenario History
docs.text: Every time the scenario changes, the Designer keeps the version before. You can compare the current scenario with any version saved since the last commit, and bring an earlier one back.

docs.title: Which versions are kept
docs.text:
A new version is saved each time the scenario changes. The list of versions names what saved it:

Name in the list When it is saved Committed version The scenario as it is in the repository: always the first version Empty (never committed) The first version of a scenario that is not in the repository yet Arianna Arianna generates or updates the scenario Sync Scenario You run Sync Scenario Manual edit You save your changes with Edit scenario Discarded changes You use Discard changes on the .scenario.md file in the file tree Restored You restore an earlier version (see below)

A save with the same text as the version before does not add a new one.

The history keeps the committed version and up to 20 later versions. When there are more, the oldest later version is dropped. The committed version always stays.

The history belongs to the chat of the file and is stored in your browser: it survives a page reload, but you do not see it from another browser.

The history starts again after a commit

When the scenario file changes in the repository — after your commit or a teammate's — the history starts again from the new committed version.

docs.title: Viewing the changes
docs.text:
The diff button (Show changes since the last commit) is at the top right of the scenario tab. It appears when the scenario has more than one version. Click it and the scenario tab shows the changes in place of the rendered scenario: on the left an earlier version, on the right the current scenario.

Fig.1 - The scenario compared with the version before

The bar above the changes has:

  • Compare with: the version on the left. By default it is the version just before the current one. Each entry shows a number, what saved it, and the time;
  • Show all / Compact: shows the whole scenario, or only the changed lines and a few lines around them;
  • Restore this version: see below.

Fig.2 - The versions of a scenario that is not in the repository yet

Click the diff button again (Hide changes) to go back to the rendered scenario.

The changes open by themselves after Arianna updates the scenario and after a sync, so you see at once what changed. They do not open after the first generation: there is nothing to compare with yet.

docs.title: Restoring a version
docs.text:
1. Open the changes and pick the version in Compare with.
  2. Click Restore this version.

The version on the left becomes the current scenario and the changes close. Nothing is lost: the text you had before the restore stays in the history as a new version, so you can restore it in the same way.

In the chat, Arianna writes which version was restored. She reads this message too, so she knows about the restore in the next requests.

Keep in mind:

  • you cannot restore while Arianna is working;
  • an Empty (never committed) version cannot be restored: Restore this version is not shown;
  • restoring the Committed version is the same as discarding the changes: the file goes back to the repository version and has nothing left to commit;
  • a restore changes only the scenario, never the XAL. If you restore the version the XAL was generated from, scenario and XAL are aligned again. Any other version makes the scenario ahead of the XAL, and Update XAL appears (see Updating XAL).

docs.title: Chat Sessions
docs.text: The AI Assistant panel can hold several chat sessions. Each session keeps its own messages; a session linked to a file also keeps its scenario and XAL. This page covers the sessions panel, the User Guide, the skills, and what you see while Arianna works.

docs.title: The sessions panel
docs.text:
Click the Chat sessions icon in the chat header to open the sessions panel. The User Guide is always first. Your sessions follow, the most recent first, each with the date of its last activity.

Fig.1 - The Chat sessions panel

Click a session to switch to it. If the session has a scenario, its scenario tab opens in the editor.

The panel lists only the sessions of the repository and branch you are connected to (see Where your sessions are kept).

docs.title: Creating a session
docs.text:
There are two kinds of session:

  • File session: linked to an XAL file. Right-click a .xal or .scenario.md file in the Repository Explorer and select New chat. There is one session per file: once you have written in it, the menu item becomes Open chat and takes you back to it. The session takes the name of the file.
  • Free session: not linked to any file. Click New in the sessions panel. If you have no sessions yet, click the New chat icon (+) in the chat header. The session is named Chat 1, Chat 2, and so on.

New is disabled when the active session is already a new, empty one.

docs.title: Resetting a session
docs.text:
Click the Reset history icon (the circular arrows) in the chat header. The messages are cleared; the linked file, the scenario and the scenario tab stay as they are. The icon is disabled when the session has no messages.

Use this to free up context when the conversation has become long but the scenario is still good.

Warning

There is no confirmation: the messages are cleared at once.

docs.title: Deleting a session
docs.text: In the sessions panel, move the mouse over a session and click the trash icon. The session and its messages are removed at once, with no confirmation. The .scenario.md and .xal files in the repository are not affected.

docs.title: Unsent messages
docs.text: Each session keeps its own unsent text and attachments. If you start writing in a session and switch to another one, you find your draft again when you come back. Drafts are lost when you reload the page.

docs.title: Where your sessions are kept
docs.text:
Sessions are saved in your browser:

  • Repository and branch: a session belongs to the repository and branch you were connected to when you created it. When you switch branch, the panel shows the sessions of the new branch. The others come back when you return.
  • Files you created: the session of a file you created and haven't committed yet follows the file when you switch branch and keep your files.
  • API key: when you change the API key, your sessions are kept (see Setup).
  • Deleted files: if you delete a file, its session stays, without that file's scenario or XAL.
  • Old sessions: sessions not used for 60 days are deleted when the Designer starts.

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text:
The User Guide is a session that is always there, pinned at the top of the sessions panel with a book icon. Ask it how to use the Designer or how the XAL language works: Arianna answers from this manual.

Fig.2 - The User Guide session

The User Guide is not linked to any file, has no Skill selector and can't be deleted. Use it to look something up without interrupting your work, then switch back to your session.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text:
Each session, except the User Guide, has a Skill selector in the chat header. A skill sets what Arianna can do in the session.

Skill Available when What Arianna does Build No scenario exists yet Guides you through describing the automaton and generates a structured scenario Update A scenario exists Helps you refine the scenario and can (re)generate the XAL; also answers operational questions, but can still modify artefacts Consult Always — chosen by hand Answers questions about the scenario and the XAL without changing them or starting any other action

Arianna selects Build or Update for you, depending on whether the session has a scenario. The other one is disabled. Select Consult when you only want to ask questions.

Click the ? icon next to the selector to open the skill legend.

Fig.3 - The skill legend

When you change skill by hand, Arianna writes a short message in the chat that says what the new skill does.

Info

Switching skill does not lose the conversation history. The next message you send will simply use the new skill's instructions.

docs.title: While Arianna works
docs.text:
While Arianna answers or runs an operation, such as Generate XAL, a progress card appears at the bottom of the chat. It shows:

  • the operation in progress, for example Answering..., and the time elapsed;
  • the last lines of Arianna's reasoning: the bottom one is what Arianna is working on now;
  • a bar with the tokens used so far;
  • Show the whole reasoning, to read the reasoning in full.

Fig.4 - The progress card while Arianna answers

Arianna runs one operation at a time: while it works, the chat header and the input box are locked.

To stop Arianna, click Cancel on the card. The chat shows Stopped. What Arianna had already saved stays: for example, a scenario saved before you clicked Cancel.

When the operation ends, the card disappears and a line Reasoning · duration · tokens stays in the chat. Click it to read the reasoning again.

Note

The texts inside the chat, such as Cancel or Update scenario from report, follow Arianna's language. This manual shows them in English.

docs.title: Guided flows
docs.text: Several actions in Arianna trigger guided flows — sequences of steps that Arianna carries out automatically or prompts you to carry out, without requiring you to navigate the interface manually.

docs.title: Post-generation flow (Generate scenario from XAL)
docs.text: After generating a scenario from an existing XAL, Arianna sends a prompt in the chat inviting you to verify consistency, with an inline Verify Scenario Consistency button. After the check, a second message sets the working direction for the session (see Generate Scenario from XAL).

docs.title: Update scenario from report
docs.text:
After every consistency check, Arianna adds a message with the Update scenario from report button. Click it and Arianna updates the scenario to fix what the report lists; the XAL is not changed. Only the button of the latest report works.

The button is disabled in Consult: switch the skill to Build or Update to use it.

docs.title: Post-sync prompt
docs.text: After Sync Scenario completes, Arianna sends a short message in the chat suggesting a consistency check, with an inline Verify Scenario Consistency button — a reminder that syncing updates the scenario to match the XAL, but does not guarantee that no details were lost.

docs.title: Automatic retry on XAL validation failure
docs.text:
When Generate XAL or Update XAL produces an invalid XAL, Arianna retries automatically, up to three attempts in all, and tells Claude the errors found so far on each attempt. The progress card shows the current attempt, for example Fixing validation errors (attempt 2/3)....

If all three attempts fail, a message in the chat provides:

  • the validation errors in plain text, so you can understand what went wrong
  • a Download XAL button for the last generated file — often nearly correct — when there is one
  • a Download .dot button, if you want to correct the GraphViz source manually

docs.title: Inline action buttons
docs.text: In some chat messages — particularly those generated by guided flows — Arianna includes inline action buttons directly in the message. These trigger the corresponding Designer action (such as Verify Scenario Consistency) without requiring you to find the button in the scenario tab. Clicking the inline button has exactly the same effect as clicking the button in the UI.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Arianna requires an Anthropic API key to function. The key is stored locally in your browser and never sent to Xautomata's servers — it is used exclusively for direct calls to the Claude API.

This page also covers the two preferences of the chat: the response language and the Claude models.

docs.title: Entering the key
docs.text:
Click the AI Assistant icon (the sparkle) in the left sidebar to open the AI Assistant panel. If no key is configured, the Connect to Claude screen appears.

Paste your Anthropic API key and click Connect. Click the eye icon next to the field to show or hide the key. The key is validated immediately; if it is invalid or has insufficient permissions, an error message is shown under the field.

If you don't have a key yet, click Get an API key → to open the Anthropic console.

Fig.1 - The Connect to Claude screen

docs.title: Removing the key
docs.text:
To clear the stored key — for example, when logging out of a shared machine — open the AI Assistant panel and click the key icon (Change API key) in the chat header. Arianna disconnects and the Connect to Claude screen appears again.

Your chat sessions are kept: when you enter a key again, you find them as you left them.

Key security

Your API key is stored in your browser's local storage. Do not use Arianna on a shared or public computer without removing the key when you are done.

docs.title: Language
docs.text:
Arianna's response language is a global preference that applies to all chat sessions. It controls both the language Claude responds in and the UI text inside the chat panel (placeholders, empty-state labels, and call-to-action messages).

To change the language, click the flag icon in the chat header. A small popover appears with the available options — currently EN (English, default) and IT (Italian). The active language has a check mark. Select one to apply it immediately; the preference is saved in a browser cookie and persists across sessions.

Fig.2 - The language popover

Note

The language setting is independent of the language you type in. Even if you write in Italian, Claude will respond in the language set here — and vice versa.

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
Arianna uses three Claude models, one for each group of tasks:

Group What it does Generation Writes the scenario and the XAL and answers in the chat. Used by the chat, Generate/Update Scenario, Generate XAL, Sync Scenario and Verify XAL Consistency. Extraction Reads the scenario and fills in the details of the XAL (Global States, Actions and Metrics) during Generate XAL. Assistance Short answers and texts: the User Guide chat and the commit message.

The Model button in the chat header shows the active configuration:

  • Recommended: the models tested by Xautomata. This is the default.
  • Custom: you changed at least one model. The button turns orange, with the tooltip Untested model configuration.

The button appears once a chat session is open (see Fig.2).

To change the models, click the Model button. The AI Assistant model configuration dialog opens:

  1. For each group, select a model from the list. The list shows the models your API key can use.
  2. Click Details under a group to see its reasoning and effort settings. These are read-only.
  3. Click Save. To go back to the recommended models, click Restore default (shown only for a custom configuration), then Save.

Fig.3 - The AI Assistant model configuration dialog

Untested configuration

With a custom configuration the dialog shows a warning: the output may differ from the recommended one. The same happens if your API key can't use a recommended model: Arianna uses another model instead, and the dialog tells you which one.

Like the language, the model configuration is saved in a browser cookie and applies to all chat sessions.

docs.title: Syncing the Scenario
docs.text: When you edit an automaton directly in the Designer — adding states, changing transitions, or adjusting parameters — the XAL changes but the scenario does not. Use Sync Scenario to update the scenario to reflect the current state of the XAL.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Sync Scenario is useful when:

  • you have refined the automaton graph manually after a generation and want the scenario to remain an accurate description
  • you want to keep the two artefacts aligned before committing

Generating a scenario for a file that has none

If you have an XAL file with no associated scenario, use Generate Scenario from XAL instead: Sync Scenario updates an existing scenario.

docs.title: When Sync Scenario appears
docs.text:
The Sync Scenario button appears in the toolbar of the scenario tab only when the XAL was edited by hand after its last generation:

  • Only the XAL changed: Sync Scenario is the only action. Click it and the sync starts.
  • Both the XAL and the scenario changed: the toolbar has a yellow frame and a warning icon, with Update XAL next to Sync Scenario. A sync would overwrite the changes made to the scenario, so it asks for confirmation first. Click Sync to go on, or Cancel.

Fig.1 - The confirmation when both files changed

When the scenario and the XAL are aligned, the button is not shown.

docs.title: Running the sync
docs.text:
Arianna reads the current XAL and updates only the parts of the scenario that correspond to what changed: it does not rewrite the whole document. While she works, the scenario tab shows a spinner and the progress card appears in the chat. If you click Cancel, nothing is changed.

The precision of the update depends on what is available:

Situation What Arianna receives Result The session knows the XAL of the last generation or sync The scenario and the changes made to the XAL since then Targeted update: only the affected sections of the scenario change The session does not know it, for example an XAL generated in another browser The scenario and the whole XAL Full update: Arianna uses the existing scenario as a reference for style and structure

docs.title: After syncing
docs.text:
The .scenario.md file is overwritten and the scenario tab opens on the changes: on the left the previous version, on the right the new one. Click the diff icon (Hide changes) at the top right to go back to the rendered scenario.

Fig.2 - The scenario tab after a sync, open on the changes

In the chat, Arianna confirms where she saved the scenario and recommends a consistency check, more strongly after a full update. Run it with Verify XAL Consistency in the scenario tab: the sync could have missed some details (see Verifying Consistency).

The XAL is the source of truth during a sync

Sync Scenario always moves the scenario towards the XAL, never the other way. If you want to update the XAL to match a changed scenario, use Update XAL instead.

docs.title: Updating XAL
docs.text: When the scenario changes after the XAL has already been generated, use Update XAL to bring the changes into the existing file without regenerating it from scratch. The edits you made by hand on the XAL are kept.

docs.title: When Update XAL appears
docs.text:
The toolbar of the scenario tab shows only the actions that apply. The first icon is the status badge: move the mouse over it to read the state.

Situation Badge Toolbar No XAL yet, or an XAL uploaded and never generated by Arianna Grey circle Generate XAL (green): see Generating XAL Scenario and XAL aligned Green check, Up to date No generate button The scenario changed since the last generation Blue arrow Update XAL (orange) The XAL was edited by hand, the scenario did not change Orange pencil Sync Scenario only: see Syncing the Scenario Both changed Yellow warning Update XAL (orange) and Sync Scenario, in a yellow frame with a warning icon

Fig.1 - Scenario and XAL both changed: Update XAL and Sync Scenario in the yellow frame

When both files changed, each action overwrites the changes of the other file: Update XAL rewrites the XAL from the scenario, Sync Scenario rewrites the scenario from the XAL. Update XAL starts at once, with no confirmation, and keeps the edits made by hand that it can carry over (see below).

docs.title: What is different from Generate XAL
docs.text:
When generating for the first time, Arianna builds the automaton graph from scratch. When updating, it receives the existing graph alongside the new scenario and produces only the changes required — preserving unchanged states, transitions, and node identifiers.

This surgical approach avoids unnecessary restructuring of an automaton that may already be partially or fully correct.

The context Arianna receives depends on what is available in the current session:

Available Context passed to Arianna .dot file from a previous generation New scenario + existing .dot (preferred — most structural context) No .dot, but XAL exists New scenario + existing XAL (used as structural reference)

The .dot file is retained internally by the session after each generation. It is not shown in the repository explorer, but it is used automatically by Update XAL when available.

The rest works as in a generation: the same steps and progress card, the file locked until the end, Cancel to stop.

docs.title: Edits made by hand
docs.text:
If you edited the XAL in the Designer after the last generation, Update XAL carries your edits into the new XAL. These are typically the values that Arianna leaves for you to complete, for example:

  • the inputs of the automata that an automaton creates;
  • the systems that a function calls (name, class and path), and its inputs and outputs;
  • the text of the queries;
  • the types and values of the Global State variables.

Functions and Global State variables that you added or removed by hand are carried over too.

Some edits are not carried over:

  • states, transitions and automata added or removed by hand: the structure of the automaton comes from the scenario, so describe them in the scenario;
  • edits on an element that the update removed;
  • edits on a value that the update changed too;
  • edits that would point to a function or a Global State variable that no longer exists;
  • all the edits, if together they would make the XAL invalid.

After the update, the chat lists the edits carried over and the ones that were not, each with the reason. Redo in the Designer the ones you still need.

docs.title: After updating
docs.text:
The XAL file is overwritten with the new version and reloaded in the graph. The status badge shows Up to date again. The chat shows the same warnings as after a generation.

If the update introduces validation errors, the same automatic retry and download fallback as a fresh generation applies.

docs.title: Verifying Consistency
docs.text: Verify XAL Consistency compares the scenario with the XAL file: Arianna checks that every element described in the scenario has a matching construct in the XAL, and reports the differences.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Run a consistency check:

  • after generating a scenario from an existing XAL, to catch any misinterpretations in the reverse generation
  • after syncing the scenario, to confirm that the update captured all the changes
  • before committing, as a final validation that the two artefacts agree

docs.title: Running the check
docs.text:
Click Verify XAL Consistency in the toolbar of the scenario tab. The button is there when the scenario and the XAL both exist. While Arianna works, the progress card shows Verifying consistency...; click Cancel to stop the check.

The report arrives as a message in the chat. Then the button disappears from the toolbar: the report is still valid while neither the scenario nor the XAL changes. When one of them changes, the button comes back.

Fig.1 - The report and the Update scenario from report button

docs.title: What the report contains
docs.text:
For each automaton, Arianna compares the scenario with the XAL: the states (initial and final), the transitions, the queries to other automata, the clocks and their resets, and the Global States. It also reports structural defects of the XAL, such as a final state that another automaton queries but can never see.

Each difference falls into one of these categories:

Category Meaning Clarifications The XAL resolves something the scenario left open, for example a check "every 30 seconds" written as a wait time. Not a problem: it tells you how the ambiguity was resolved. Inconsistencies Something in the XAL that matches no reasonable reading of the scenario, or that cannot work. These are problems. Missing Something the scenario describes that has no match in the XAL, often left out while refining the automaton in the Designer. Technical conventions Standard parameters missing where an automaton creates another one.

A category with no items is left out of the report.

The check does not cover the XAL syntax, which is validated when the XAL is generated, nor other XAL files that the automaton calls.

docs.title: Acting on the report
docs.text:
Decide which of the two files is right for each item:

  • The XAL is right, the scenario must change: click Update scenario from report under the report. Arianna updates the scenario to fix what the report lists; the XAL is not changed. You can also use Sync Scenario when the XAL was edited by hand.
  • The scenario is right, the XAL must change: edit the automaton in the Designer, or describe the change to Arianna and then use Update XAL.

Update scenario from report works only on the latest report, and only while the scenario is the one that was checked. It is disabled in the Consult skill: switch to Build or Update to use it.

docs.title: Clock Variables
docs.text:
Clock variables are timer identifiers used in transitions to measure elapsed time and enforce time-based conditions.

To view and manage clock variables, click Clock Vars (clock icon) in the left sidebar. The panel shows all clocks defined for the active automaton. It is active only when an automaton is open.

Fig.1 - The Clock Vars panel

docs.title: Adding a clock
docs.text:
1. Click + at the top right of the panel. A new row appears with the name field open.
  2. Type the name and press Enter.

A clock has only a name, used in clock constraints and clock resets on transitions. Unlike global state variables, clocks have no type, value or star — they are purely time counters.

The name follows the same rules as global state variables: only letters, digits and _, not starting with a digit, and no two clocks of the same automaton with the same name. If the name is not valid, a red message appears under the field.

To rename a clock, click its name. If you clear the name, the clock is deleted.

Every change is saved automatically and can be undone with Ctrl+Z, as in the Global States panel.

docs.title: Deleting a clock
docs.text:
Click the trash icon on the clock's row to remove it.

Warning

The designer does not check whether the clock is still used: it deletes it even when a transition refers to it in a clock constraint or a clock reset. Remove the clock from those transitions first. A clock constraint that names a clock that does not exist is invalid for the interpreter.

docs.title: Using clocks in transitions
docs.text:
Once a clock is defined, it becomes available in the Clocks section of the transition configuration panel:

  • Clock constraint — a condition such as waitClock >= 5 min that must hold for the transition to fire
  • Clock Reset Variables — the clocks to restart from zero when the transition fires

See Metric Value and Clocks for the steps. For a full explanation of how clocks drive time-based logic, see Clocks and Time.

docs.title: Global State Variables
docs.text:
Global state variables store data that persists across the entire lifecycle of an automaton instance. They act as the automaton's memory — holding values that states and transitions can read and write.

To view and manage global state variables, click Global States (globe icon) in the left sidebar. The panel shows all variables defined for the active automaton. It is active only when an automaton is open.

Fig.1 - The Global States panel, with the variable status starred

docs.title: Adding a variable
docs.text:
1. Click + at the top right of the panel. A new row appears with the name field open.
  2. Type the name and press Enter.
  3. Click + Type and + Value to fill the other fields.

Each variable has:

Field Description Name The identifier used to reference the variable throughout the automaton. Required. Type The data type: string, int, long, bool, object, or a collection such as list[string] or map[string, int]. Optional. Value The starting value of the variable when an instance of the automaton starts. Optional. ★ Starred variable: the interpreter writes its value in the log messages about the instance, for example when a function fails. Click the star to turn it on or off.

The name must contain only letters, digits and _, and must not start with a digit. Two variables of the same automaton cannot have the same name. If the name is not valid, a red message appears under the field and the variable is not saved until you correct it.

docs.title: Editing a variable
docs.text:
Click a name, a type or a value to edit it in place. Press Enter or click elsewhere to confirm.

  • If you clear the type or the value, the field is removed from the variable.
  • If you clear the name, the variable is deleted.

To delete a variable, click the trash icon on its row.

Every change is saved automatically: while the panel saves it, Applying changes… appears at the top right of the canvas. You can undo and redo the changes with the buttons at the bottom of the canvas, or with Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y (see The Interface).

Warning

The designer does not check whether a variable is still used before you delete or rename it. Update the parameters, paths and clock constraints that use it first.

While Arianna regenerates the file of the automaton, the panel is read-only and shows Regenerating this automaton....

docs.title: How variables are used
docs.text:
Global state variables are referenced in:

  • Metric input and output parameters — passing values to a metric function or capturing its results
  • Action input and output parameters — providing context to an action or storing its output
  • TransitionNew input parameters — passing data to a child automaton at the moment it is spawned
  • Clock constraints — when a variable stores a threshold value used in a time condition

Info

In the parameters, the XAL refers to a variable by its name. In clock constraints, queries, and the file or automaton chosen from Global States, it refers to it as this.GLOBALSTATE_<name>. The designer adds this prefix for you — you never need to type it manually (see Referencing variables).

docs.title: Managing Automata
docs.text:
You create, rename and delete automata from the Explorer in the left sidebar.

Right-click a XAL file or an automaton, or click the ⋮ button at the end of its row, to open its menu. Right-clicking an automaton tab on the canvas opens the same automaton actions.

Fig.1 - The menu of an automaton in the Explorer

To create a new XAL file, click + at the bottom of the Explorer. The new file already contains one automaton with the same name as the file.

docs.title: Creating an automaton
docs.text:
Right-click the XAL file and select New automaton. The Create Automaton dialog opens.

Fig.2 - The Create Automaton dialog

Field Description File The XAL file in which the automaton is created. Pre-filled with the file you right-clicked. Click the file icon to select a different one. Name The name of the automaton. Required. Use letters and numbers only. It must be unique in the file. Pattern Not available yet.

Click Confirm. The automaton opens in a new tab, with a single state init that is already the initial state.

docs.title: Renaming an automaton
docs.text:
