Right-click the automaton and select Rename. The automaton opens in its tab and the Edit Automaton dialog opens.

Type the new name and click Save. The same rules as for creation apply: letters and numbers only, unique in the file.

To undo a rename, press Ctrl+Z in the automaton tab.

Warning

The designer does not update the references to the old name. Any other automaton that references this one by name, through a TransitionNew or a metric query, must be updated manually.

docs.title: Deleting an automaton
docs.text:
Right-click the automaton and select Delete. Confirm with Delete. The tab of the automaton closes.

You cannot undo a deletion with Ctrl+Z. What happens next depends on the automaton:

  • An automaton that is in the repository stays in the Explorer, marked as removed, until you commit. To get it back, right-click it and select Restore automaton, then confirm with Restore. The automaton goes back to the version in the repository.
  • An automaton you created and never committed is lost.

The deletion reaches the repository only when you commit.

docs.title: Discarding the changes to an automaton
docs.text:
When an automaton has changes that are not committed, its menu also shows Discard changes. See Commit and Push.

Note

While Arianna regenerates a XAL file, the actions on that file and on its automata are disabled. See Generating XAL.

docs.title: Files in the Explorer
docs.text:
The Explorer in the left sidebar shows the folders and files of the connected branch: the XAL files, their scenarios (.scenario.md) and the files you add, Java files included. A folder appears only when it contains a XAL file or a scenario.

To connect a repository or open a file, see Opening a File.

docs.title: File colors
docs.text:
The color of a name tells you its state compared with the repository.

Color Meaning Default Same as in the repository Green A new file or automaton, not in the repository yet Yellow A file or automaton with changes that are not committed Red, struck through An automaton you deleted: it is removed from the repository at the next commit

A name struck through with a warning icon is a file that the designer cannot read. You cannot open it.

docs.title: The file menu
docs.text:
Right-click a file, or click the ⋮ button at the end of its row, to open its menu.

Fig.1 - The menu of a new XAL file

The items depend on the file:

Item Shown for What it does New chat / Open chat XAL files and scenarios Opens the Arianna chat of the file. See Chat Sessions. New automaton XAL files Adds an automaton to the file. See Managing Automata. Download New files Saves the file on your computer. Rename New XAL files Renames the file. See Renaming a file. Remove file New files Removes the file from the Explorer, after a confirmation. Its tabs close. Discard changes Scenarios with changes Brings the scenario back to the version in the repository.

A file that is already in the repository cannot be downloaded, renamed or removed from the Explorer.

Note

While Arianna regenerates a XAL file, the items that change the file or its scenario are disabled. See Generating XAL.

docs.title: Adding files
docs.text:
At the bottom of the Explorer:

  • + opens the New XAL file dialog. Type a name and click Create. The .xal extension is added for you. The new file contains one automaton with the same name and opens in a tab.
  • Upload File loads a file from your computer: a XAL file, a scenario or a Java file.

A new file starts at the top of the repository. If a file with the same name is already there, the new one gets a number: pump.xal becomes pump(1).xal.

The Explorer has no command to create a folder. Move the file into an existing folder (see below), or choose its folder when you commit: a folder that does not exist yet is created by the commit. See Choosing the folder of a new file.

docs.title: Moving a file
docs.text:
You can move only the new files.

  1. Drag the file onto a folder. The folder is highlighted.
  2. To move a file out of its folders, drop it on the Move to root / box that appears below the files while you drag.

The Explorer scrolls when you drag the file near its top or bottom edge.

  • A XAL file and its scenario stay together: when you move one, the other moves too.
  • When you move a Java file, the XAL file that uses it is updated with the new path.
  • If the folder already has a file with the same name, the moved file gets a number.

A new XAL file whose scenario is already in the repository cannot leave that folder, and the other way around. The designer shows Cannot move file.

docs.title: Renaming a file
docs.text:
You can rename only the new XAL files.

  1. Open the menu of the file and select Rename. The Rename file dialog shows the name without the extension.
  2. Type the new name and click Rename.

The name can contain only letters and numbers: spaces, dashes, underscores and other characters are not accepted. The .xal extension stays.

The scenario of the file is renamed with it, and the Arianna chat follows the file. If the name is already taken in the folder, the file gets a number.

A new XAL file whose scenario is already in the repository cannot be renamed. The designer shows Cannot rename.

docs.title: Reloading the files
docs.text:
The arrow next to the EXPLORER title reloads the files from the repository. It closes all the tabs and clears the undo history.

If you have changes that are not committed, the designer asks for confirmation first: the reload discards them. Click Reload anyway to go on, or Cancel. The new files you added stay in the Explorer.

docs.title: The Interface
docs.text:
The XAL Designer interface is organized into four main areas that work together during an editing session.

Fig.1 - The XAL Designer interface with an automaton open and a state selected

docs.title: Top bar
docs.text:
The top bar provides access to global controls.

Element Description Eye (left) Full immersion: hides the top bar and collapses the left sidebar, so the canvas gets more room. Click the thin strip at the top to show the bar again. Repository / branch Shows the connected repository and branch. Click it to choose another repository or branch. Before you connect, it reads Connect to VCS. Upload arrow Opens the Commit & Push dialog. It is visible only when a repository is connected, and active when there are changes to commit. Play (right) Run-time instance: opens the Xautomata run-time platform in a new browser tab.

docs.title: Left sidebar
docs.text:
The sidebar provides access to all editing panels and tools. Hover an icon to see its name, click it to open the corresponding panel.

The double arrow at the top collapses the open panel to the icons only, and expands it again.

Icon Name Description Tree File Opens the Explorer: the file and automaton tree of the connected repository Globe Global States Manages the global state variables of the active automaton Clock Clock Vars Manages the clock variables of the active automaton Microchip New State Adds a new state to the active automaton Two arrows New Transition Adds a new transition to the active automaton Store Marketplace (Coming soon) Sparkle AI Assistant Opens the Arianna chat panel User (bottom) User Shows your account, with Logout (or Connect to VCS when you are not connected) and the Dark Mode (beta) switch

Global States, Clock Vars, New State and New Transition are active only when an automaton is open.

To create, rename or delete an automaton, right-click a file or an automaton in the Explorer (see Managing Automata). At the bottom of the Explorer, Upload File loads a XAL file from your computer, and + creates a new XAL file. See Files in the Explorer.

docs.title: Canvas
docs.text:
The canvas occupies the central area of the interface.

It displays one of two views depending on the active tab:

  • Overview — the correlation graph showing all automata in the repository and their relationships
  • Automaton diagram — the interactive graph of a specific automaton, with states as nodes and transitions as edges

You can pan the canvas by clicking and dragging on an empty area, and zoom with the scroll wheel. Individual nodes can be dragged to reposition them.

At the bottom of the canvas, two buttons provide undo and redo for the changes to the automaton. You can also press Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y (Cmd on macOS).

docs.title: Right panel
docs.text:
The right panel shows the configuration form for the currently selected element on the canvas.

It opens automatically when you click on a state node or a transition edge. It closes when you click on an empty area of the canvas or press the × button in the panel header.

The panel content changes depending on what is selected:

  • State selected — shows the state Metadata, Action, and Metric sections
  • Transition selected — shows the transition Metadata, Clocks, and Parameters sections

Changes made in the panel are applied immediately to the automaton, with a short debounce delay.

docs.title: Tabs
docs.text:
Each open automaton appears as a tab in the tab bar, next to the persistent Overview tab. When you work with Arianna, the scenario tab sits right after Overview.

  • Click a tab to switch the canvas to that automaton. Hover it to see the file path.
  • Drag a tab to change its position.
  • A dot on a tab signals uncommitted changes. When you hover the tab, the dot becomes the × button.
  • Click ×, or click the tab with the middle mouse button, to close it. Closing a tab does not discard its changes: see Commit and Push.
  • Right-click a tab for Close, Close all other tabs and the same actions as the file menu in the Explorer.

docs.title: Opening a File
docs.text:
When you open the XAL Designer, a welcome dialog lets you choose where your XAL files come from: a repository, or your computer.

Fig.1 - The welcome dialog

If the dialog does not appear, for example on your first visit, when the cookie banner is shown, click Connect to VCS in the top bar.

docs.title: Connecting to a repository
docs.text:
1. Select GitHub or GitLab. The other providers are shown greyed out: they are not available yet.
  2. Enter your Username and a Personal Access Token, then click Connect. Back returns to the provider list.
  3. In the top bar, click Select repository. The Select Repository & Branch dialog opens.
  4. In Repository, type part of the name to filter the list. A lock marks the private repositories. When two repositories have the same name, the list shows the owner too.
  5. In Branch, choose the branch. The first branch of the list is selected for you.
  6. Click Connect. The designer loads the files of the branch.

Fig.2 - The Select Repository & Branch dialog

If the login fails, an error message appears and you can try again. If you accepted the cookies, the designer remembers the login for seven days: the next time you open it, you are already connected.

docs.title: The Explorer
docs.text:
Once connected, the Explorer in the left sidebar shows the folders and files of the branch. Click a XAL file to expand it and see the automata it contains. Click an automaton to open it as a new tab on the canvas (see Tabs).

The arrow next to the EXPLORER title reloads the files from the repository. To add, move or rename files, see Files in the Explorer.

Fig.3 - The Explorer with a XAL file expanded

docs.title: Switching repository or branch
docs.text:
Click the repository and branch in the top bar. The Select Repository & Branch dialog opens with the current choice: select another repository or branch and click Connect.

  • The open tabs are closed.
  • If you have uncommitted changes, the designer asks for confirmation: Connect anyway discards them.
  • If you have files that are not in the repository yet, for example files you uploaded, the Local files dialog asks what to do with them: Keep leaves them in the Explorer as new files, Discard deletes them, together with their Arianna chat.
  • While Arianna is regenerating a XAL file, you cannot switch: wait for the end, or cancel the regeneration from the chat.

To leave the repository, click Disconnect in the same dialog. If you have uncommitted changes, the designer asks for confirmation first. To log out of the provider, use Logout in the User menu at the bottom of the left sidebar.

docs.title: When the session expires
docs.text: If the login with the provider expires, for example because the token was revoked or reached its expiry date, the designer shows the VCS Session Expired notification and a warning icon next to the EXPLORER title. To continue, click Connect to VCS in the top bar and log in again.

docs.title: Working in the browser
docs.text:
Select Start in browser to work without a repository. The Explorer starts empty. At its bottom:

  • Upload File loads a file from your computer: a XAL file, a scenario (.scenario.md) or a Java file. If the Explorer already has a file with the same name, the new one is renamed.
  • + creates a new XAL file.
  • The download button appears when there are new files. It opens the Download Files dialog: select the files and click Download.

Warning

In the browser, your files live only in the browser tab. A page reload keeps them, but closing the tab loses them. Download your files before you close the tab.

You can connect to a repository later, with Connect to VCS in the top bar. Your files stay in the Explorer as new files, ready to commit.

docs.title: Correlation Types
docs.text:
The Process Overview shows three types of relationships between automata. Each type has its own line style and color, and you can show or hide each type independently.

The Legend (the ⓘ button at the top left of the graph) and the filter panel (top right) use different names for two of the types:

Legend Filter panel Line SQL-like SQL-Based Solid blue New Invocation Dashed purple Family Tree Family Tree Dotted orange

In dark mode the colors are lighter.

Fig.1 - The legend: the three line styles and the three node shapes

docs.title: SQL-like
docs.text:
A SQL-like correlation (solid blue line) connects an automaton to another whose state it reads through a query.

When an Action or a Metric of automaton A has a query that reads the table of automaton B, the designer draws an SQL-like edge from A to B. This represents a data dependency: A observes B's state to drive its own transitions.

The designer finds automaton B from the table name, which joins the file name and the automaton Id (see Queries). It looks for the file first in the folder of automaton A and in its parent folders, then in the whole repository. If it does not find the file or the automaton, B is drawn as a cloud.

When you select a node, the SQL-like edges show the Id of the Actions and Metrics that contain the query. When more than one query reads the same automaton, the edge lists all of them.

This is the most common type of correlation in monitoring scenarios.

docs.title: New
docs.text:
A New correlation (dashed purple line) connects a parent automaton to a child automaton that it starts.

When an automaton has a TransitionNew or a TransitionNewMulti that starts another automaton, the designer draws a New edge from the parent to the child. The child is found from the Target File and the Target Automaton of the transition (see Spawning Child Automata). If the Target Automaton comes from a global state variable, the child is drawn as an ellipse.

This represents a lifecycle dependency: the parent creates the child, and the child then runs on its own.

docs.title: Family Tree
docs.text:
A Family Tree correlation (dotted orange line) connects an automaton to another automaton that it runs as a subprocess.

When an Action or a Metric of automaton A has the type Automaton (see Type Automaton), the designer draws a Family Tree edge from A to the automaton that the function runs. Unlike a TransitionNew, the function waits for the called automaton to finish, and receives its output values.

This type of correlation is less common than the other two.

docs.title: Filters and orphan nodes
docs.text:
In the filter panel, under Show Correlations, a switch for each type shows or hides its edges.

An orphan is an automaton that has no connections in the current view: a standalone automaton, or an automaton whose connections are all of a hidden type. The Show Orphans switch, Enabled or Disabled, includes or excludes the orphan nodes from the graph. It is available only when at least one correlation type is shown.

Fig.2 - The filter panel

docs.title: Opening an Automaton
docs.text: You can open an automaton for editing from two places: the Process Overview graph and the Explorer.

docs.title: From the Process Overview
docs.text:
The Overview tab displays the correlation graph of all automata in the loaded files.

Double-click a node in the graph to open the corresponding automaton on the canvas. It appears as a new tab in the tab bar. The Explorer does not need to be open.

Single-clicking a node only highlights its connections — it does not open the automaton. Make sure to double-click.

Note

Only the rounded rectangles can be opened. Clouds (automata whose file is not among the loaded files) and ellipses (automata chosen from a global state variable) have no file to open. See Node shapes.

docs.title: From the Explorer
docs.text:
Click File (tree icon) in the left sidebar to open the Explorer.

The Explorer shows the folder structure of the connected repository and the files you uploaded. Click a XAL file to expand it and show the automata it contains. Each automaton is listed below its file with a graph icon.

Click an automaton name to open it on the canvas. If its tab is already open but not active, the click switches to it. If its tab is the active one, the click closes the tab.

An automaton that you deleted and did not commit yet stays in the Explorer until the commit, but you cannot open it.

Fig.1 - An expanded XAL file in the Explorer showing its automata

docs.title: Working with multiple automata
docs.text:
Each automaton you open appears as a separate tab. You can have several automata open at the same time and switch between them by clicking their tabs.

Opening the same automaton a second time switches to its existing tab rather than opening a duplicate.

To move, close and manage the tabs, see Tabs.

docs.title: Navigating back to the Overview
docs.text: Click the Overview tab at any time to return to the correlation graph. The automaton tabs remain open in the background — your work is not lost.

docs.title: Reading the Process Overview
docs.text:
The Overview tab displays a graph of all the automata in the loaded files and the relationships between them.

This view gives you a bird's-eye picture of the entire automation system — which automata exist, how they are connected, and which ones reference automata that are not in the loaded files.

Fig.1 - The Process Overview graph, with the legend open on the left and the filters on the right

If no repository is connected and no file is uploaded, the tab shows Select a repository or upload a file to explore the process overview.

The graph updates by itself when the files change: when you edit an automaton, upload a file, or reload the files of the Explorer.

docs.title: Node shapes
docs.text:
Each node in the graph represents an automaton. The shape of the node indicates where the automaton is defined. Click the ⓘ button at the top left of the graph to open the Legend.

Shape Legend name Meaning Rounded rectangle Automaton An automaton defined in a loaded file. The node shows the folder, the file and the automaton. Cloud External file An automaton referenced by file name, but the file, or the automaton in it, is not among the loaded files. The node shows the file and the automaton. Ellipse Global State variable The automaton is chosen at run time from a global state variable. The node shows the variable name with a globe icon.

A cloud does not always mean an error: the automaton can exist in another repository and run at platform level. If you expected to find it in the repository, check the file name and the automaton Id.

Long folder, file and automaton names are cut with .... Hover a node to see the full names.

docs.title: Node border colors
docs.text:
The border color of a node reflects its connections in the graph.

Border color Meaning Green Only outgoing connections — a source automaton Red Only incoming connections — a leaf automaton. Clouds and ellipses are usually red, because they only receive connections. Blue Both incoming and outgoing connections, or no connections at all (an orphan)

The legend draws all the shapes with a blue border: it explains the shapes, not the colors.

docs.title: Interacting with the graph
docs.text:
Single-click a node to highlight its connections. The connected edges become thicker, and the SQL-like edges show the names of the Actions and Metrics that contain the query. Click an empty area of the graph to remove the highlight.

Fig.2 - The Patcher automaton selected: its edges are thicker and show their labels

Double-click a rounded rectangle to open the automaton on the canvas as a new tab. Clouds and ellipses cannot be opened. See Opening an Automaton.

The graph supports panning and zooming. You can drag the nodes to rearrange the layout. The positions are not saved: the designer draws the graph again, from the same starting layout, when the files change, when you change a filter or the theme, and when you reload the page.

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
Use the panel at the top right of the graph to show or hide each correlation type, and to show or hide the orphan nodes — automata that have no connections in the current view.

If no correlation is left to show, the graph shows No correlations to show.

Info

For a description of the three correlation types and of the filters, see Correlation Types.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: If the designer cannot read a file to compute its correlations, the Overview shows the error Error calculating correlations for followed by the file path. The automata of that file are missing from the graph. Open the file to find and correct the error.

docs.title: Commit and Push
docs.text: When you have finished editing an automaton, you can publish your changes back to the connected repository using the Commit & Push function.

docs.title: The unsaved changes indicator
docs.text:
While you are editing, a dot indicator appears on the tab of any automaton that has uncommitted changes. This includes structural edits (adding or removing states and transitions), configuration changes, and layout changes such as moving nodes on the canvas.

Fig.1 - The dot indicator signals uncommitted changes on a tab

docs.title: Opening the commit dialog
docs.text:
Click the upload/commit button in the top bar to open the Commit & Push dialog. The button is active only when a repository and a branch are connected and there is at least one change to commit.

If you edited by hand an XAL that has Java functions, the designer first brings its Java stub file up to date. The updated .java file then appears among the changes. See Java Stubs.

Fig.2 - The Commit & Push dialog

The dialog shows:

Section Description Changes included All the pending changes, with the number of selected changes out of the total. Each change has a toggle to include it in the commit. No change is selected when the dialog opens: use Select All, or the single toggles. Commit message A text field for the commit message, pre-filled with Commit from XAL Designer. Write your own message, or click Generate with AI. Validation results The result of the validation run on the selected files. A green checkmark and 0 files with errors means that the files are valid and ready to commit.

docs.title: Choosing the changes
docs.text:
Each change has a tag that tells you what it is:

Tag Meaning new file A file that is not in the repository yet. new A new automaton in a file of the repository. modified An automaton you changed. removed An automaton you deleted. layout only An automaton where only the position of the nodes changed. Click the arrow next to the tag to discard these changes. regenerating A file that Arianna is generating again. You can commit it when the generation ends.

docs.title: Files that go together
docs.text: An XAL file, its scenario (.scenario.md) and its Java stub file (.java) are committed together. When you select one of them, the others are selected too. When you clear one of them, the others are cleared too.

docs.title: Choosing the folder of a new file
docs.text:
A new file shows its folder as a chip before the file name. The chip shows root when the file is at the top of the repository.

  1. Click the chip.
  2. Type the folder path, for example processes/pumps. A folder that does not exist yet is created by the commit.
  3. Press Enter, or click outside the field.

An XAL file and its scenario stay in the same folder: when you move one of them, the other moves too. You can put the .java file in any folder: the XAL is updated to point to the new path.

If the XAL or the scenario is already in the repository, the chip of the new file is locked: the file stays next to the other one. Hover over the chip to see why.

The chip turns red, and you cannot commit, when:

  • the path contains characters that are not allowed (use letters, numbers, _ - . ( ) and /);
  • a file with the same path is already in the repository;
  • another new file goes to the same path.

docs.title: Generating the message with AI
docs.text:
Click Generate with AI to let Arianna write the commit message. Arianna reads the selected changes and, when there is one, the scenario of each XAL. The message follows the conventional commits format, for example feat(pump): add the pump station automaton.

  • The button is available when an API key is set (see Setup), at least one change is selected, and Arianna is not answering in the chat.
  • The generated message replaces the text in the field. You can edit it before you commit.
  • If you close the dialog while the message is being generated, the generation stops.

The button next to Generate with AI shows the language of the message, with its flag. Click it to choose EN or IT. This language is separate from the language of Arianna: at first it is the same, then the designer remembers your choice.

docs.title: Validation before commit
docs.text:
Before the commit is sent, the platform validates all included XAL files against the schema and runtime rules. This is the authoritative validation — it is the same check that runs when the platform loads an automaton.

If any file contains errors, the validation results section shows the number of files with errors. Resolve the issues before committing. If you need to commit anyway, the button becomes Commit & Push anyway. The same happens when the validator cannot be reached: the files were not checked.

Note

The designer may show form validation warnings (such as field format messages) that are independent of the backend validation. A file that passes backend validation is considered correct, even if the designer shows minor warnings.

docs.title: Completing the commit
docs.text:
Once the validation passes, click Commit & Push to publish your changes. The changes are pushed to the selected branch of the connected repository.

The dot indicator disappears from the affected tabs after a successful commit.

docs.title: Closing a tab with uncommitted changes
docs.text:
Closing a tab does not discard its changes: they stay in the list of changes to commit, and you find them again when you reopen the automaton.

To discard the changes to an automaton, right-click it in the file panel and choose Discard changes. Confirm with Discard: the automaton goes back to the version in the repository.

Warning

Discarded changes cannot be recovered from within the designer.

docs.title: Configuring State Actions
docs.text:
An action associated with a state defines an operation the automaton performs when it enters that state. Actions interact with external systems — APIs, ERP platforms, warehouse management systems, or any other integration target. An action can also start another automaton.

To configure an action, select a state on the canvas and open the Action panel in the state sidebar.

Fig.1 - The Action panel of a state, with a Java method chosen

The panel saves every change by itself, like the rest of the sidebar. If the state name is not valid, the panel shows Changes are kept but not saved until the state metadata is valid. Fix the name in Metadata to save them (see Creating a State).

docs.title: The warning indicator
docs.text: When a state has no action, the Action header shows a ⚠ icon. It is only a reminder: it does not prevent the automaton from being saved or committed.

docs.title: Query
docs.text:
The Query field is optional. It retrieves data from the platform before the action runs. Choose how to fill it:

  • Manual: type the query in the editor (see Query Syntax).
  • Global State: select a global state variable that holds the query.

When the action has a query and parameters, list[string] and Query result appear above the parameters in Action Sign: the result of the query is passed to the action.

docs.title: Action Data
docs.text:
The Type field sets what the action runs:

Type What it runs Object A Java method Automaton Another automaton

Changing Type clears the file, the class and the Target Type.

docs.title: Type Object
docs.text:
1. In the file field, click the file icon and choose the .java file from the repository. To type the path instead, click the pencil.
  2. In Class, select the class. If the file has only one class, the designer selects it for you.
  3. In Action, select the method. The list shows only the public static methods of the class, with their parameter types.
  4. In Action Sign, link each parameter of the method to a global state variable of the automaton. For string and int parameters, the list shows only the variables of the same type.
  5. In Action Return, select the global state variable that receives the value returned by the method.

Below the parameters, Action Code shows the code of the method. You cannot edit it here.

Changing Class clears Action.

If the file is not in the repository, the panel shows The file appears to be missing from the repository. Code preview is disabled. You can still configure the action: Class and Action become text fields, and you add the parameters by hand (see Parameters typed by hand). The file may exist in the platform's runtime environment, and the automaton still works.

Info

The classes available for actions depend on the platform deployment. For a list of standard implementations, contact the XAUTOMATA delivery team.

docs.title: Type Automaton
docs.text:
Use Target Type to choose where the automaton to start comes from.

File

  1. In File*, choose the .xal file that contains the automaton.
  2. In Automaton*, select the automaton. The list shows the automata of the file.
  3. In Min Wait, type the minimum wait in seconds.
  4. In Action Sign, link the input variables of the called automaton to the variables of the current one.
  5. In Action Return, link the output variables of the called automaton to the variables of the current one.

Global States

The file and the automaton come from two global state variables of type string:

  • File*: the variable that holds the file;
  • Automaton*: the variable that holds the automaton.

You add the parameters by hand.

Changing Target Type clears the file, the automaton and the parameters.

docs.title: Parameters typed by hand
docs.text: When the designer cannot read the parameters from a file, you add them one by one: type the name of the parameter, select the local variable and click +. To remove a parameter, click ×. You cannot add the same parameter twice: the panel shows Parameter already added.

docs.title: Removing the action
docs.text: Click Reset at the bottom of the panel. The form is cleared and the state no longer has an action. To get it back, press Ctrl+Z.

docs.title: Automatic changes
docs.text:
When you open a state, the designer may adjust some values so that the form can show them. A notification tells you:

  • Action was changed: a saved path was adapted to the form.
  • Automaton was reset: the selected automaton no longer exists in the file. Select a new one, or change the file.

docs.title: Creating a State
docs.text: States are the nodes of the automaton diagram. You can create a new state at any time while an automaton is open on the canvas.

docs.title: Adding a state
docs.text:
1. Click New State in the left sidebar. The configuration panel opens on the right, with the name NewNode.
  2. In the Name field, type the name of the state.

The state appears on the canvas as soon as the name is valid. From then on the panel saves every change by itself: there is no save button.

Fig.1 - A new state on the canvas, with its configuration panel

To give up before the state appears, click × in the panel header. Nothing is added.

docs.title: Naming a state
docs.text:
The name must follow these rules:

  • it is required;
  • it contains only letters and numbers, with no spaces or underscores;
  • it is not NewNode;
  • it is not used by another state of the same automaton.

If the name breaks a rule, the panel shows a message next to the field. An existing state keeps your other changes, but saves them only when the name is valid again.

When you rename a state, the transitions connected to it follow the new name.

docs.title: Setting the state type
docs.text:
Use the Type selector to mark the state as Initial or Final. Leave both unselected for an intermediate state.

  • Initial makes this the starting state of the automaton. An automaton has only one initial state: if you select Initial on another state, that state becomes the initial one and the previous one becomes an intermediate state.
  • Final marks a terminal state. An automaton can have several final states. When the automaton reaches a final state, it stops processing.

You cannot change the type of the initial state, and you cannot delete it. To replace it, select Initial on another state.

Reset clears the name and the type. On the initial state, it leaves the type as it is.

The star next to the state name marks the state as starred (see States).

docs.title: Saving and automatic changes
docs.text:
While the panel saves a change, Applying changes… appears at the top right of the canvas, and a thin line runs under the top bar.

When you open a state, the designer can adjust some values of its Action or Metric so that the form can show them. A notification tells you: Action was changed or Metric was changed. See Actions and Metrics.

To undo a change, click the undo button at the bottom of the canvas or press Ctrl+Z (see The Interface).

docs.title: Moving states on the canvas
docs.text:
Drag a state node to reposition it on the canvas. The layout is not constrained: place nodes wherever makes the diagram easiest to read.

Note

Moving a node counts as a change, and the tab shows a dot. If you only moved nodes, the Commit and Push dialog marks the automaton as layout only.

docs.title: Deleting a state
docs.text:
Select the state on the canvas, click the trash icon in the top-right corner of the panel and confirm with OK.

Deleting a state also removes all the transitions connected to it. To get them back, press Ctrl+Z.

docs.title: Configuring State Metrics
docs.text:
A metric associated with a state defines what the automaton observes while it is in that state. The values returned by the metric determine which outgoing transition fires next.

To configure a metric, select a state on the canvas and open the Metric panel in the state sidebar.

Fig.1 - The Metric panel of a state, with two symbols and a Java file chosen

The panel saves every change by itself, like the rest of the sidebar. If the state name is not valid, the panel shows Changes are kept but not saved until the state metadata is valid. Fix the name in Metadata to save them (see Creating a State).

On the canvas, a state with a metric shows a chart icon followed by the metric name.

docs.title: The warning indicator
docs.text: When a state has no metric, the Metric header shows a ⚠ icon. It is only a reminder: it does not prevent the automaton from being saved or committed.

docs.title: Symbols
docs.text:
The symbols are the values the metric can return. Each symbol is a possible outcome that an outgoing transition can wait for.

To add a symbol, type it in New Symbol and click +. To remove a symbol, click × next to it.

  • A symbol starts with a letter and contains only letters, digits and hyphens (-).
  • You cannot add the same symbol twice: the panel shows Symbol already added.

Info

On each outgoing transition, the Metric Value list shows the symbols of the input state's metric (see Metric Value and Clocks). Add the symbols here first, then choose them on the transitions.

docs.title: Query
docs.text:
The Query field is optional. It reads data from the platform before the metric runs, for example the global state of another automaton. Choose how to fill it:

  • Manual: type the query in the editor.
  • Global State: select a global state variable that holds the query.

A query that reads the status of the Patcher automaton in patcher.xal:

SELECT GLOBALSTATE_STATUS FROM patcher_Patcher WHERE groupLabel = 'this.GROUPLABEL'

The table name joins the file name and the automaton name. For the rules, see Query Syntax.

When the metric has a query and parameters, list[string] and Query result appear above the parameters in Metric Sign: the result of the query is passed to the metric.

When a query is configured, the state node on the canvas shows a table icon in its top-right corner.

docs.title: Metric Data
docs.text:
Metric Data works like Action Data in the Action panel: the same Type (Object or Automaton), the same fields and the same steps. See Configuring State Actions. Only the names change:

Action panel Metric panel Action Metric Action Sign Metric Sign Action Return Metric Return Action Code Metric Code

docs.title: Which value is the symbol
docs.text:
A metric returns the symbol that chooses the outgoing transition. In Metric Return, the round button next to a return value marks the value that holds the symbol.

  • With Type Object, the method has one return value: it is the symbol, and it is also written to the global state variable you select.
  • With Type Automaton, the called automaton can return more values. Click the round button next to the one that holds the symbol.

docs.title: Removing the metric
docs.text:
Click Reset at the bottom of the panel. The form is cleared, symbols included, and the state no longer has a metric. To get it back, press Ctrl+Z.

Warning

The transitions that leave this state keep their Metric Value, but no metric returns it any more.

docs.title: Automatic changes
docs.text:
When you open a state, the designer may adjust some values so that the form can show them. A notification tells you:

  • Metric was changed: a saved path was adapted to the form.
  • Automaton was reset: the selected automaton no longer exists in the file. Select a new one, or change the file.

docs.title: Creating a Transition
docs.text: Transitions connect states and define the conditions under which the automaton moves from one state to another.

docs.title: Adding a transition
docs.text:
1. Click New Transition in the left sidebar. The configuration panel opens on the right, with empty fields.
  2. In the Metadata section, choose the Input State (where the transition starts) and the Output State (where it arrives). The options are the states of the current automaton.

The transition appears on the canvas as soon as both states are set. From then on the panel saves every change by itself: there is no save button.

Fig.1 - A new transition from waitingIdle to relocated, with its configuration panel

To give up before the transition appears, click × in the panel header. Nothing is added.

Note

A transition can have the same state as both input and output. This creates a self-loop, drawn as a small loop on the state: the automaton remains in that state until a different condition is met.

docs.title: Configuring the transition
docs.text:
The panel has three sections:

Section Contents See Metadata Input and output state, Metric Value, Target Min Wait, Ignore Min Wait Metric Value and Clocks Clocks Clock constraints and clock resets Metric Value and Clocks Parameters Target File, Target Automaton and the variables passed to the child automaton Spawning Child Automata

While the panel saves a change, Applying changes… appears at the top right of the canvas. To undo a change, press Ctrl+Z, also on a transition you have just created.

docs.title: The transition type
docs.text:
The panel title shows the type of the transition. On a new transition, the type follows the fields you fill in:

  • Transition: the standard type.
  • TransitionNew: you set a Target File and a Target Automaton in the Parameters section.
  • TransitionNewMulti: you also set the loop variables.

For a full description of each type and when to use it, see Transition Types.

docs.title: Transitions on the canvas
docs.text:
Each transition is an arrow from the input state to the output state:

  • the label shows the Metric Value;
  • a transition that starts a child automaton shows ✚ and the name of the target automaton (✚✚ for a TransitionNewMulti);
  • a clock symbol marks a clock constraint, ↺ a clock reset. Hover the arrow to see them;
  • two transitions in opposite directions between the same states are drawn as two separate arrows.

docs.title: Deleting a transition
docs.text: Select a transition on the canvas by clicking its edge or label, click the trash icon in the top-right corner of the panel and confirm with Delete. To get it back, press Ctrl+Z.

docs.title: Metric Value and Clocks
docs.text:
The Metric Value field and the Clocks section of the transition panel decide when a transition fires. You can use them alone or together.

Fig.1 - A self-loop on exception: Metric Value, Ignore Min Wait and a clock constraint

docs.title: Metric Value
docs.text:
The Metric Value is the value the metric of the input state must return for the transition to fire. It is available on a Transition, not on a TransitionNew.

Choose it from the list. The options are the values declared on the metric of the input state (see Configuring State Metrics). If the input state has no metric, or its metric declares no values, the list is empty.

Without a Metric Value, the transition does not look at the metric: it fires as soon as its clock constraints hold.

Warning

Two transitions from the same input state cannot have the same Metric Value and the same clock constraints: the automaton could not tell which one to take. In that case the field shows Metric value already in use.

docs.title: Clock constraints
docs.text:
A clock constraint makes the transition wait for, or stop waiting after, a given time. It compares a clock of the automaton with a value: waitClock >= 5 min holds once five minutes have passed since waitClock was last reset.

To add one, in the Clocks section:

  1. choose the Clock Variable: the clocks of the automaton (see Clock Variables);
  2. choose the Operator: <, <=, > or >=;
  3. in Value, type a whole number, or choose a Global State of the automaton to compare with its value;
  4. optionally choose the Unit: sec, min or hour. Without a unit, the value is in seconds;
  5. click +.

The + button stays disabled until clock, operator and value are set. A value that is neither a number nor a Global State shows Value must be a number or a global state.

The constraint appears below as a chip; a Global State in it shows its icon. To remove a constraint, click × on its chip.

A transition can have several clock constraints: all of them must hold at the same time.

docs.title: Clock Reset Variables
docs.text:
Clock Reset Variables lists the clocks to restart from zero when the transition fires. Choose one or more clocks of the automaton; each one appears as a tag you can remove.

Reset a clock on the transition that enters the waiting phase, and constrain it on the transitions that leave it.

docs.title: Ignore Min Wait
docs.text: The Ignore Min Wait switch lets the transition fire without waiting for the min wait of the automaton. See Min Wait and Ignore Min Wait.

docs.title: Combining conditions
docs.text:
When a transition has both a Metric Value and clock constraints, both must hold: the metric has returned that value, and all constraints are met.

A common pattern is the timeout: one transition handles the expected value, another leaves the state when a clock exceeds a limit. In Fig.1 the self-loop on exception fires only when the metric returns dispatchingAlive and waitClock has reached five minutes.

docs.title: Spawning Child Automata (TransitionNew)
docs.text: A TransitionNew does two things when it fires: it moves the automaton to the output state, and it starts a new child automaton. This is how you build automaton families.

docs.title: Creating a TransitionNew
docs.text:
1. Create a transition as usual (see Creating a Transition).
  2. In the Parameters section, set the Target File and the Target Automaton.

As soon as both are set, the panel title becomes TransitionNew. If you also fill in the loop row, it becomes a TransitionNewMulti (see below).

You choose this while you create the transition: a saved Transition does not show the Parameters section.

Fig.1 - A TransitionNew that starts RelocateDB from patcher.xal and passes it DbHostName

docs.title: Target File
docs.text:
The Target File is the XAL file that contains the child automaton. Use the switch above the field to choose where it comes from:

  • File: pick a .xal file of the repository from the list. Click the pencil to type the name instead.
  • Global States: pick a Global State of the current automaton. When the transition fires, the file is the value that variable holds at that moment. Use a string variable.

The child can also be in the same file as the parent.

docs.title: Target Automaton
docs.text:
Choose the automaton to start from the Target Automaton list. The options are in two groups:

  • Automatons: the automata of the Target File;
  • Global States: the Global States of the current automaton. When the transition fires, the automaton is the one named by the value of that variable.

The field is required: without it the panel shows A target automaton is required.

docs.title: Target Min Wait
docs.text:
Target Min Wait is the min wait of the child, in seconds: the minimum time the child spends in each of its states before it can leave it. Leave it empty or at 0 for no wait.

See Min Wait and Ignore Min Wait.

docs.title: Input parameters
docs.text:
The input parameters copy values from the parent to the child when the child starts. Each row pairs two variables:

Field Description Target Variable The Global State of the child that receives the value. The options are the Global States of the Target Automaton. Local Variable The Global State of the parent the value is read from.

If the Target Automaton comes from a Global State, the designer cannot know the child's variables and the Target Variable list is empty: type the name.

To add a row, choose both variables and click +. To remove a row, click ×. If you fill in only one of the two, the panel warns Select values for both fields.

The value is copied once, when the child starts: later changes in the parent do not reach the child.

Info

The child must declare the Target Variable in its own Global State, with a type compatible with the Local Variable. Otherwise the value is not passed.

docs.title: Starting one child per item (TransitionNewMulti)
docs.text:
A TransitionNewMulti starts one child for each item of a list. Fill in the loop row of the input parameters:

Field Description Loop Local Variable A list Global State of the parent. Loop Target Variable The Global State of each child that receives its item of the list.

When the transition fires, the list is read and one child starts for each item. All children also receive the normal input parameters, and all of them use the same Target Min Wait.

On a TransitionNewMulti both loop fields are required: if one is empty, the panel shows Loop variables are required.

docs.title: Starting more than one child
docs.text:
Each TransitionNew starts one child (or one per item, for a TransitionNewMulti). To start different children, chain the TransitionNew through states: for example, one from A to B that starts the first child, and one from B to C that starts the second.

Warning

Do not give a state two transitions that can fire at the same moment, for example two TransitionNew without clock constraints. The automaton cannot choose between them and stops with an error.

docs.title: Monitoring the child
docs.text:
After the start, the parent follows the child through a Metric. Its query reads the child's Global State from the child's table, <FileName>_<AutomatonId>, filtered by groupLabel:

SELECT GLOBALSTATE_STATUS FROM patcher_RelocateDB WHERE groupLabel = 'this.GROUPLABEL'

When the child reaches the state the parent waits for, the Metric returns the matching value and the parent's transition fires. See Query Syntax for the table names and the groupLabel binding.

For the whole pattern, see Automaton Families.

docs.title: On the canvas
docs.text: A TransitionNew is a dashed arrow labeled ✚ and the name of the target automaton. A TransitionNewMulti shows ✚✚. See Transition types on the canvas.

docs.title: Transition Types
docs.text:
The type of a transition decides what it does when it fires and which fields its panel shows. The panel title shows the type.

You do not choose the type from a list: on a new transition it follows the fields you fill in (see Creating a Transition).

docs.title: Transition
docs.text:
The standard transition moves the automaton from the input state to the output state.

Its panel shows:

  • Metric Value: the value the metric of the input state must return;
  • Ignore Min Wait: lets the transition fire without waiting for the min wait (see below);
  • Clock Constraints and Clock Reset Variables.

A transition without a Metric Value and without clock constraints fires as soon as the automaton is in the input state.

See Metric Value and Clocks for these fields.

docs.title: TransitionNew
docs.text:
A TransitionNew starts a child automaton and moves the parent to the output state.

Its panel shows:

  • Target File and Target Automaton: the automaton to start;
  • Target Min Wait: the min wait of the child, in seconds (see below);
  • the Input Parameter rows: the values passed to the child when it starts;
  • Clock Constraints and Clock Reset Variables.

A TransitionNew has no Metric Value: it fires on its clock constraints alone, and the min wait never delays it.

See Spawning Child Automata for the target and the parameters.

Info

For how parent and child automata work together, see Automaton Families.

docs.title: TransitionNewMulti
docs.text: A TransitionNewMulti works like a TransitionNew, but starts one child for each item of a list. The list is a Global State of the parent, chosen in the loop row of Input Parameter.

docs.title: TransitionX
docs.text:
TransitionX is an older form that puts a transition and the start of a child in one element. The interpreter still runs it, and the designer draws it as a plain arrow, but you cannot create one from the designer.

To get the same behavior, draw a Transition and a TransitionNew between the same two states. At run time they become a single transition: it fires on the Metric Value of the Transition, and uses the clock constraints and resets of the TransitionNew.

docs.title: Min Wait and Ignore Min Wait
docs.text:
The min wait is the time, in seconds, an automaton must spend in a state before it can leave it. It is set by whoever starts the automaton: for a child automaton, it is the Target Min Wait of the TransitionNew that started it. With no min wait, or 0, nothing is delayed.

Ignore Min Wait exempts one transition from it: the transition can fire as soon as its conditions hold.

docs.title: Transition types on the canvas
docs.text:
Appearance Type Solid arrow Transition Dashed arrow, no ✚ Transition with Ignore Min Wait on Dashed arrow, label ✚ and the target automaton TransitionNew Dashed arrow, label ✚✚ and the target automaton TransitionNewMulti Solid arrow, no label TransitionX

The label of a Transition shows its Metric Value, plus a clock symbol for a clock constraint and ↺ for a clock reset. Hover an arrow to see the details.

docs.title: Actions Reference
docs.text: Actions are defined within the <Functions> element and represent operations the automaton performs when it enters a state associated with that action.

docs.title: Action element
docs.text:
<Action Id="createOrderInERP" Type="object">
  <System
    Name="createOrderInERP"
    Class="erp.TeamSystemConnector"
    Path="/erp/src/TeamSystemConnector.java"/>
  <Input>
    <Parameter LocalVariable="erpApiEndpoint" TargetVariable="apiEndpoint"/>
    <Parameter LocalVariable="orderData" TargetVariable="orderData"/>
  </Input>
  <Output>
    <Parameter LocalVariable="erpOrderId" TargetVariable="erpOrderId"/>
  </Output>
</Action>

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text: Attribute Required Description Id Yes Unique identifier within the <Functions> element. Referenced by state IdAction attributes. Type Yes What the action runs: object for a Java method, automaton for another automaton. See Type automaton. MinWait No Only with Type="automaton": the min wait, in seconds, of the automaton the action starts. See Min Wait and Ignore Min Wait. The interpreter ignores it on object actions.

docs.title: <System>
docs.text:
Specifies what the action runs.

Attribute Type="object" Type="automaton" Name The name of the method The Id of the automaton to start Class The fully qualified name of the class The name of the XAL file that contains the automaton Path The path of the .java file in the repository Not used

The method must be public static. The interpreter loads the class from the .jar files installed on the platform: the .java file in the repository is not required at runtime.

docs.title: <Query>
docs.text: An optional query on the state of other automata. The interpreter runs it before the action and passes the result to the method as its first argument, a list[string]. See Query Syntax.

docs.title: <DataSource>
docs.text:
An optional reference to a data source of the platform, by its code. The interpreter passes the data source to the method as an argument, after the query result.

<DataSource Code="erp-production"/>

docs.title: <Input>
docs.text:
Lists the global state variables passed to the action. See Parameter Passing.

<Input>
  <Parameter LocalVariable="orderId" TargetVariable="orderId"/>
</Input>

docs.title: <Output>
docs.text:
Lists the global state variables where the action writes its result. See Parameter Passing.

<Output>
  <Parameter LocalVariable="erpOrderId" TargetVariable="erpOrderId"/>
</Output>

docs.title: Type automaton
docs.text:
With Type="automaton" the action starts another automaton as a step of the current one: the current automaton waits for it to finish (see Automaton Families).

<Action Id="relocate" Type="automaton" MinWait="60">
  <System Name="RelocateDb" Class="patcher.xal"/>
  <Input>
    <Parameter LocalVariable="DbHostName" TargetVariable="DbHostName"/>
  </Input>
  <Output>
    <Parameter LocalVariable="relocationResult" TargetVariable="result"/>
  </Output>
</Action>

Name and Class can also take the value of a global state variable, written as this.GLOBALSTATE_<name>: the automaton and the file are read from that variable when the action runs.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Both <Input> and <Output> are optional. An action that has no side effects on the automaton's global state may omit them.
  • The designer warns if the .java file is not found in the current repository, but the automaton can still work if the class exists at runtime.

Info

For information on which system classes are available in your deployment, contact the XAUTOMATA delivery team.

docs.title: Automaton Reference
docs.text: The <Automaton> element is the top-level container for a single automaton definition within an XAL file.

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text: Attribute Required Description Id Yes Unique identifier of the automaton within the file. Used by TransitionNew elements and metric queries to reference this automaton.

docs.title: Child elements
docs.text:
The child elements can appear in any order (see File Structure).

Element Required Description <Functions> Yes Contains <Action> and <Metric> definitions. Must be present even if empty. <States> Yes Contains all <State> definitions. <InitialState> Yes Declares the starting state using IdState. <Transitions> Yes Contains all transition elements. <GlobalState> No Contains <Variable> definitions for shared state. <Clocks> No Contains <Variable> definitions for clock timers. <FinalStates> No Contains <FinalState> elements declaring terminal states.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
An automaton with two states and one transition:

<Automaton Id="SimpleMonitor">
  <Functions/>
  <GlobalState>
    <Variable Name="status" Type="string"/>
  </GlobalState>
  <Clocks/>
  <States>
    <State Id="Watching"/>
    <State Id="Alerted"/>
  </States>
  <InitialState IdState="Watching"/>
  <FinalStates>
    <FinalState IdState="Alerted"/>
  </FinalStates>
  <Transitions>
    <Transition
      IdInputState="Watching"
      IdOutputState="Alerted"
      MetricValue="critical"
      IgnoreMinWait="true"/>
  </Transitions>
</Automaton>

docs.title: Multiple automata in one file
docs.text:
A single XAL file commonly contains a family of related automata. The parent automaton references children by their Id in TransitionNew elements, or in actions and metrics with Type="automaton", and children reference the parent through metric queries.

<XAL>
  <Automaton Id="Parent">
    ...
    <Transitions>
      <TransitionNew
        IdInputState="Init"
        IdOutputState="Running"
        Path="myfile.xal"
        Type="Child"
        MinWait="300"/>
    </Transitions>
  </Automaton>

  <Automaton Id="Child">
    ...
  </Automaton>
</XAL>

All automaton IDs within the same file must be unique.

docs.title: XAL File Structure
docs.text: An XAL file is an XML document that contains one or more automaton definitions. All automata in a file share the same namespace and can reference each other by name.

docs.title: Root element
docs.text:
The root element of every XAL file is <XAL>. It contains one or more <Automaton> elements.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<XAL>
  <Automaton Id="MyAutomaton">
    ...
  </Automaton>
  <Automaton Id="AnotherAutomaton">
    ...
  </Automaton>
</XAL>

docs.title: Automaton structure
docs.text:
Each <Automaton> element contains the following child elements, all at the same level and in any order:

Element Required Description <Functions> Yes Defines the metrics and actions used by the automaton <States> Yes Lists all states <InitialState> Yes Declares the starting state <Transitions> Yes Contains all transition definitions <GlobalState> No Declares shared variables <Clocks> No Declares clock variables <FinalStates> No Lists terminal states

docs.title: Order of elements and attributes
docs.text:
The order of elements and attributes has no effect on the interpreter. The XAL Designer always writes them in the same order, so that two versions of a file are easy to compare:

  • inside <Automaton>: GlobalState, Clocks, Functions, States, InitialState, FinalStates, Transitions;
  • inside <Functions>: all the actions, then all the metrics;
  • inside <Transitions>: all the Transition elements, then TransitionNew, TransitionNewMulti and TransitionX.

When you save a file written by hand or by another tool, the designer rewrites it in this order. The content does not change.

docs.title: File naming and organization
docs.text:
XAL files use the .xal extension. Multiple automata are typically grouped in a single file when they form a family — a parent automaton and its related children.

Files are organized in a directory structure within the repository. TransitionNew elements reference child automata by file name (Path) and automaton ID (Type). See Transitions.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
XAL files are validated by the XAUTOMATA platform at load time, against the schema of the XAL language. A file that does not pass validation is not loaded, and none of its automata is executed. Elements or attributes that the schema does not know, a missing required element or a reference to a state that does not exist all make the file invalid.

The XAL Designer performs backend validation as part of the commit process, before pushing changes to the repository. See Commit and Push for details.

docs.title: Global State
docs.text:
The <GlobalState> element declares variables that persist throughout the entire lifecycle of the automaton instance. These variables form the automaton's working memory.

<GlobalState>
  <Variable Name="orderId" Type="string"/>
  <Variable Name="retryCount" Type="int" Value="0"/>
  <Variable Name="shopifyApiEndpoint" Type="string" Desc="Shopify API endpoint"/>
</GlobalState>

docs.title: Variable attributes
docs.text: Attribute Required Description Name Yes Identifier used to reference the variable throughout the automaton. Unique within the automaton. Type No Data type: string, int, long, bool, object, or a collection such as list[string] or map[string,int]. The interpreter uses it to convert Value and to match the parameters of Java methods. Value No Default value assigned when the automaton is instantiated Desc No Human-readable description. Used as documentation only. IO No Marks the variable as an input (I), output (O), or both (I/O). Documentation only: the interpreter does not check it when passing parameters. Starred No If true, the interpreter adds the value of the variable to its log messages about the instance, for example when a function fails.

docs.title: Referencing variables
docs.text:
Global state variables are referenced in two ways:

  • By name, in the LocalVariable of a <Parameter> in Input, Output and LoopInput blocks (see Parameter Passing).
  • As this.GLOBALSTATE_<name>, where the XAL expects a value: in clock constraints, in queries, in Path and Type of a TransitionNew or TransitionNewMulti, and in Name and Class of the <System> of a function with Type="automaton". The interpreter replaces it with the current value of the variable.

In the designer, you choose the variable from a list and the designer adds the this.GLOBALSTATE_ prefix for you.

docs.title: Clocks
docs.text:
The <Clocks> element declares timer variables used in transition conditions.

<Clocks>
  <Variable Name="clk_retry"/>
  <Variable Name="clk_handshake"/>
</Clocks>

docs.title: Clock variable attributes
docs.text:
Attribute Required Description Name Yes Identifier used in ClockConstraint and ClockReset elements

Clocks have no type, value, or description — they are pure timers. A clock starts counting from zero when the instance starts, and again every time a <ClockReset> element on a transition resets it.

The name minWaitClockVariable is reserved: the interpreter uses it for the min wait, and rejects a clock with that name.

docs.title: Clock constraint syntax
docs.text:
<ClockConstraint ClockExp="clk_retry < 10 min"/>
<ClockConstraint ClockExp="clk_auth >= this.GLOBALSTATE_authTimeout"/>

The ClockExp attribute contains the comparison expression. Use XML-escaped operators:

Operator XML encoding < < <= <= > > >= >=

The right-hand side of the expression is one of:

  • a whole number, optionally followed by a unit: sec, min, hour or day (e.g. 5 min, 2 hour). Without a unit, the number is in seconds;
  • a global state variable, written as this.GLOBALSTATE_<name>: its value is read when the constraint is checked, in seconds unless a unit follows.

The expression can contain only clocks of the automaton, global state variables, whole numbers, units, the operators above and +, -, *, /. Any other name, such as a constant that is not a clock or a global state variable, makes the constraint invalid, and the interpreter reports an error in its log.

Note

The designer offers sec, min and hour. day is accepted by the interpreter, but you have to write it by hand in the XAL.

docs.title: Clock reset
docs.text:
<ClockReset ClockVar="clk_retry"/>

Resets the specified clock to zero when the transition fires. Multiple <ClockReset> elements can appear on a single transition.

docs.title: Metrics Reference
docs.text: Metrics are defined within the <Functions> element and represent data-reading functions the automaton uses to observe the state of other automata or monitored objects.

docs.title: Metric element
docs.text:
<Metric Id="checkPickingConfirmation" Type="object">
  <System
    Name="checkPickingConfirmation"
    Class="wms.WaterFallConnector"
    Path="/wms/src/WaterFallConnector.java"/>
  <Query>
    SELECT GLOBALSTATE_STATUS
    FROM scenario_FollowerManager
    WHERE groupLabel = 'this.GROUPLABEL'
  </Query>
  <Input>
    <Parameter LocalVariable="wmsPickingListId" TargetVariable="pickingListId"/>
  </Input>
  <Output>
    <Parameter LocalVariable="confirmedQuantities" TargetVariable="confirmedQuantities"/>
  </Output>
  <Enumeration>
    <Const Value="confirmed"/>
    <Const Value="pending"/>
    <Const Value="error"/>
  </Enumeration>
</Metric>

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text: Attribute Required Description Id Yes Unique identifier within <Functions>. Referenced by state IdMetric attributes. Type No What the metric runs: object for a Java method, automaton for another automaton, as for actions. MinWait No Only with Type="automaton": the min wait, in seconds, of the automaton the metric starts. The interpreter ignores it on object metrics.

docs.title: <System>
docs.text:
Specifies what the metric runs, as for actions (see Actions).

Attribute Description Name The method name to invoke (with Type="automaton", the automaton to start) Class The fully qualified class name (with Type="automaton", the XAL file) Path The implementation file path

docs.title: <Query>
docs.text: A SQL-like expression that reads the target automaton's or object's state. See Query Syntax for the full specification.

docs.title: <Input>
docs.text: Maps global state variables into the metric's input parameters.

docs.title: <Output>
docs.text: Maps the metric's return values back into the automaton's global state. The MetricSymbol attribute on <Output> can optionally specify the variable name used to expose the metric value externally.

docs.title: <Enumeration>
docs.text:
Defines the set of values the metric can return. Each <Const Value="..."/> declares one possible return value.

<Enumeration>
  <Const Value="confirmed"/>
  <Const Value="pending"/>
  <Const Value="error"/>
</Enumeration>

Enumeration values are used as MetricValue conditions on outgoing transitions from states associated with this metric. Only transitions whose MetricValue matches a declared constant will fire.

docs.title: Metric vs Action
docs.text:
Both metrics and actions use <System>, <Input>, and <Output>. The key difference is their purpose:

  • A metric reads state and returns a value from the enumeration, driving transitions.
  • An action performs an operation and may update global state variables, but does not return an enumeration value that drives transitions directly.

In the XAL Designer, metrics are configured in the Metric section of the state panel, and actions in the Action section.

docs.title: Parameter Passing Reference
docs.text: Parameters allow automata to exchange data — between a parent and a child at spawn time, and between an automaton and its metric or action functions.

docs.title: Parameter element
docs.text:
<Parameter LocalVariable="orderId" TargetVariable="orderId"/>
Attribute Required Description LocalVariable Yes The name of the variable in the current automaton's global state, without any prefix TargetVariable Yes The name of the variable in the target context: the variable of the child automaton, or the parameter of the Java method Position No Not used by the interpreter: the arguments of a method follow the order of the <Parameter> elements

docs.title: Input parameters
docs.text:
<Input> blocks pass values into a function or child automaton.

In a metric or action with Type="object", input parameters become the arguments of the Java method. The interpreter passes them by position, in the order of the <Parameter> elements: the order must match the signature of the method. TargetVariable holds the name of the method parameter, for readability. If the function has a <Query> or a <DataSource>, their values come first (see Actions).

<Action Id="getOrder" Type="object">
  <System Name="getOrderFromShopify" Class="ecommerce.ShopifyConnector" Path="/src/ShopifyConnector.java"/>
  <Input>
    <Parameter LocalVariable="shopifyApiEndpoint" TargetVariable="apiEndpoint"/>
    <Parameter LocalVariable="orderId" TargetVariable="orderId"/>
  </Input>
</Action>

In a TransitionNew, TransitionNewMulti or a function with Type="automaton", input parameters copy values from the parent's global state to the child's global state at instantiation. The value of LocalVariable in the parent becomes the starting value of TargetVariable in the child:

<TransitionNew IdInputState="newOrder" IdOutputState="instantiatedOperator"
  Path="ecommerce_backoffice.xal" Type="Operator">
  <Input>
    <Parameter LocalVariable="shopifyApiEndpoint" TargetVariable="shopifyApiEndpoint"/>
    <Parameter LocalVariable="shopifyCredentials" TargetVariable="shopifyCredentials"/>
  </Input>
</TransitionNew>

docs.title: Output parameters
docs.text:
<Output> blocks capture values returned by a metric or action and write them into the automaton's global state:

<Metric Id="checkPickingConfirmation" Type="object">
  <System Name="checkPickingConfirmation" Class="wms.WaterFallConnector" Path="/src/WaterFallConnector.java"/>
  <Output>
    <Parameter LocalVariable="confirmedQuantities" TargetVariable="confirmedQuantities"/>
  </Output>
</Metric>

With Type="object":

  • with one output parameter, the value returned by the method is written into its LocalVariable;
  • with more than one, the method returns a map whose keys are the LocalVariable names, and each value is written into the matching variable.

With Type="automaton", when the child finishes, the value of each TargetVariable in the child is written into the matching LocalVariable of the parent.

For the value that drives the transitions of a metric, see Metrics.

docs.title: Loop input parameters
docs.text:
<LoopInput> is used exclusively in TransitionNewMulti. It contains a single <Parameter> pointing to a list variable in the parent's global state. The transition iterates over the list and spawns one child instance per item:

<TransitionNewMulti IdInputState="Start" IdOutputState="Cycle"
  Path="patcher.xal" Type="RecycleAppPools" MinWait="300">
  <LoopInput>
    <Parameter LocalVariable="AppPools" TargetVariable="AppPool"/>
  </LoopInput>
</TransitionNewMulti>

Each spawned child receives one element from the AppPools list as the value of its AppPool variable.

docs.title: Variable resolution
docs.text:
In a <Parameter>, LocalVariable is always the plain name of a global state variable, for example DbHostName:

<Parameter LocalVariable="DbHostName" TargetVariable="DbHostName"/>

The this.GLOBALSTATE_ prefix is used elsewhere, where the XAL expects a value (see Referencing variables).

docs.title: Special input values
docs.text:
Instead of a global state variable, LocalVariable can name one of these values, prepared by the interpreter:

LocalVariable Type Value XAL_EXCEPTION_DESCRIPTION string The detail of the last error raised by an action or a metric of the instance XAL_SELF_DESCRIPTION string The description of the current instance XAL_GLOBAL_STATE_VARS map[string,string] All the global state variables of the instance, with their values as text

TargetVariable gives the name the value takes in the child automaton or in the method.

docs.title: Query Syntax
docs.text: Metrics and some actions use a SQL-like query to read data from the platform's runtime database. This page describes the query format and the conventions used throughout XAL files.

docs.title: Basic structure
docs.text:
A query follows standard SQL SELECT syntax:

SELECT <column> FROM <table> WHERE groupLabel = 'this.GROUPLABEL'

The most common form reads the global state status of another automaton:

SELECT GLOBALSTATE_STATUS FROM scenario_FollowerManager WHERE groupLabel = 'this.GROUPLABEL'

docs.title: Table naming convention
docs.text:
Each automaton has its own table. The table name joins the XAL file name and the automaton Id with an underscore:

<FileName>_<AutomatonId>

<FileName> is the XAL file name without the .xal extension, unchanged. <AutomatonId> is the Id attribute of the target automaton.

Examples:

File Automaton Table name scenario.xal FollowerManager scenario_FollowerManager patcher.xal Dispatcher patcher_Dispatcher

Upper and lower case do not matter in the table name. patcher_Dispatcher, PATCHER_DISPATCHER and Patcher_dispatcher read the same table.

Note

This applies only to table names in queries. In the Path of a TransitionNew, write the file name exactly, with the same case.

Warning

Do not use hyphens in the name of a XAL file that other automata query. The platform cannot create a table for a file like drone-leader.xal, so every query on it fails.

docs.title: The groupLabel binding
docs.text:
The WHERE groupLabel = 'this.GROUPLABEL' clause is mandatory in all automaton state queries. It binds the query to the specific instance of the target automaton that is running on the same monitored object as the querying automaton.

Without this binding, the query would return results from all running instances of the target automaton, regardless of which object they belong to.

this.GROUPLABEL is a runtime placeholder — the platform substitutes it with the actual group label of the current instance at execution time.

docs.title: Querying specific columns
docs.text:
In addition to GLOBALSTATE_STATUS, queries can retrieve other global state variables:

SELECT GLOBALSTATE_STATUS as "status", GLOBALSTATE_RelocatedDBs as "RelocatedDBs"
FROM PATCHER_RelocateDb
WHERE groupLabel = 'this.DbHostName'

The as alias maps the column to the output parameter that receives the value in the automaton's global state.

docs.title: Alternative WHERE clauses
docs.text:
Some queries use a specific global state variable in the WHERE clause instead of this.GROUPLABEL:

WHERE groupLabel = 'this.DbHostName'

This targets the instance associated with the value stored in the DbHostName variable of the current automaton's global state.

docs.title: Queries in the XAL Designer
docs.text:
In the XAL Designer, the query is entered in the Query field of the Metric configuration section. The designer does not validate the query syntax — correctness is verified by the platform at runtime.

When a state has a query configured on its metric, a grid icon appears in the top-right corner of the state node on the canvas.

docs.title: States Reference
docs.text: States are defined within the <States> element and represent the phases of the automaton's lifecycle.

docs.title: State element
docs.text:
<State
  Id="Waiting"
  IdMetric="checkStatus"
  IdAction="sendNotification"
  Starred="true"
  style='{"x":120,"y":-340}'/>

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
Attribute Required Description Id Yes Unique identifier of the state within the automaton. Referenced by transitions and the initial/final state declarations. IdMetric No ID of the <Metric> function to observe while the automaton is in this state. IdAction No ID of the <Action> function to execute when the automaton enters this state. Starred No If true, marks the state as starred. See Starred states. style No JSON object storing the canvas position of the node (x, y). Managed automatically by the designer — do not edit manually.

A state can have both IdMetric and IdAction defined simultaneously.

docs.title: Initial state
docs.text:
Exactly one state must be declared as the initial state:

<InitialState IdState="Init"/>

The IdState attribute must match the Id of an existing state in the automaton.

docs.title: Final states
docs.text:
Terminal states are declared in the <FinalStates> element:

<FinalStates>
  <FinalState IdState="Completed"/>
  <FinalState IdState="Failed"/>
  <FinalState IdState="Exception"/>
</FinalStates>

An automaton stops processing when it reaches any of its final states. Final states typically have no outgoing transitions.

docs.title: State color coding in the designer
docs.text: Color State type Green Initial state Bordeaux Final state Blue Intermediate state

docs.title: Starred states
docs.text:
A starred state marks a phase that the platform must know about. When the platform's process queue is configured, at every cycle the interpreter sends to it the instances that are in a starred state, with their data.

The Starred attribute is set through the ★ toggle in the state configuration panel of the XAL Designer (see Creating a State).

Note

Starred on a global state variable is a different thing: it adds the value of the variable to the interpreter's log messages about the instance (see Global State).

docs.title: Transitions Reference
docs.text: Transitions define how the automaton moves between states. Four transition types are available, each with its own element name and set of attributes.

docs.title: Common attributes
docs.text:
All transition types share these attributes:

Attribute Required Description IdInputState Yes ID of the state the automaton must be in for the transition to fire IdOutputState Yes ID of the state the automaton moves to when the transition fires IgnoreMinWait No If true, the transition can fire without waiting for the min wait of the automaton. See Min Wait and Ignore Min Wait.

docs.title: Transition
docs.text:
The standard transition. Fires when a metric value matches and/or clock constraints are satisfied.

<Transition
  IdInputState="Waiting"
  IdOutputState="Processing"
  MetricValue="confirmed"
  IgnoreMinWait="true">
  <ClockConstraint ClockExp="clk_wait < this.GLOBALSTATE_maxWait"/>
  <ClockReset ClockVar="clk_wait"/>
</Transition>

Additional attributes:

Attribute Description MetricValue The metric return value that triggers the transition

Child elements:

Element Description <ClockConstraint ClockExp="..."/> A time-based condition. Multiple elements allowed: all must hold. See Clock constraint syntax. <ClockReset ClockVar="..."/> Resets the specified clock when the transition fires. Multiple elements allowed.

docs.title: TransitionNew
docs.text:
Spawns a child automaton and moves to the output state. Used to build automaton families.

<TransitionNew
  IdInputState="Init"
  IdOutputState="Processing"
  Path="ecommerce_backoffice.xal"
  Type="Operator"
  MinWait="300"
  IgnoreMinWait="true">
  <Input>
    <Parameter LocalVariable="shopifyApiEndpoint" TargetVariable="shopifyApiEndpoint"/>
    <Parameter LocalVariable="orderId" TargetVariable="orderId"/>
  </Input>
</TransitionNew>

Additional attributes:

Attribute Required Description Path Yes File name of the XAL file containing the target automaton. It can be the same file.
